mr president, first of all i would like to express my condolences and solidarity with the victims of the earthquake in haiti. this devastating earthquake, which comes after the four hurricanes last year, should not make us forget the situation that this country was already suffering before the earthquake, with 80% of the population living in poverty. with the highest infant mortality rate in america, poverty, violence and exodus were already part of the daily lives of much of the haitian population. in this context it is essential not only to send humanitarian aid but also to ensure that, when haiti is no longer covered, the effort continues and that haiti develops in a sustainable, coordinated and balanced way.
what would you think, lords, if police officers accompanied by the cameras of the main television stations in the country broadcast your arrest live? how would they feel if they were accused of belonging to an armed gang, arrested, held incommunicado for five days, had their assets blocked and were thrown in jail for a period of up to a year and a half for being managers of the only newspaper then published in basque and which ended up being closed without a trial? in addition, most of the detainees have reported that they were tortured. but how would you feel if seven years later, despite the prosecutor's request to dismiss the case for lack of evidence, you were still awaiting trial? how about there's another part of the case, the economic case, pending another trial? this is the situation in which ten people, most of them journalists, have been living since the spanish national court decided, in february 2003, to close egunkaria without a trial. after this tour, a trial is taking place in these weeks which, given the time elapsed and the circumstances described, is anything but fair to the accused and their rights.

high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy/vice-president of the commission. − mr president, honourable members, this is an important opportunity to raise the situation in iran. the european union wants normal relations with iran, and our efforts on the nuclear issue are part of that. in this context, i will continue, in my capacity as high representative, the role of my predecessor, javier solana, in the international talks with iran. iran is an important country with a deep history and rich culture, and a remarkably talented population. the films and books coming out of iran are impressive, the level of education of women is high, there is a capacity for public debate and the young population is vibrant and active. in many ways, iranian society has the hallmarks and the capacity of a free society. the threat to the society has been reflected in the turmoil that followed what many in iran saw as a fraudulent election last year. that, of course, is a matter for the iranians. our concern is that international norms and standards on civil and political rights must be respected. in this respect, i am deeply concerned over the reports of violent suppression of demonstrations and arbitrary detentions in tehran and other iranian cities during the recent ashura commemorations at the end of december. the use of violence against demonstrators seeking to exercise their freedom of expression and rights of assembly is not acceptable. these are universal human rights that must be respected and those detained for peacefully exercising those rights should be released. i also note with deep concern that many arrests seem to have targeted human rights defenders and journalists, and that many detained are denied access to legal representation and contact with their families. iran must live up to its international obligations and treat detained persons in accordance with international human rights standards. another recent issue is the detention of another 12 members of the baha’i religious community. these people must be assured a just, open and fair trial in accordance with international standards. the eu has spared no opportunity to ask the iranian government to respect those international obligations which they freely and voluntarily adhered to. we issue public statements and use other diplomatic means. we work through the united nations: the general assembly adopted a resolution condemning the situation only last month. we will make full use of the upcoming review of iran which will be held at the un human rights council in geneva in early february. on the nuclear issue, we regret that tehran has not followed up on the last meeting between javier solana and jalili, the chief negotiator, on 1 october in geneva. we all assessed that the meeting was positive. but, in effect, iran has now rejected a draft agreement proposed by the iaea and has been refusing to pursue talks on the nuclear issue. the eu and its negotiating partners are all committed to finding a diplomatic solution to the iranian nuclear issue, and to that end we must continue to implement the dual-track approach. we need a serious engagement in meaningful talks from tehran’s side. our objective remains to build confidence that the nuclear programme is exclusively for peaceful purposes. the confidence deficit was further increased by the revelation that iran has been building another enrichment facility without informing the iaea in due time. in addition, iran continues not to cooperate fully with the iaea and not to respect its international obligations. it is vital that the eu and the international community stand united behind the negotiating effort, including by supporting that effort through appropriate measures. the widest possible unity is key if we are to achieve our objective. if iran sets out on a more constructive course on the nuclear issue and on regional stability in general, it could play an important role in the middle east and gulf region, which would reflect its rightful place and proud history. in conclusion, the challenges posed by iran weigh very heavy in my portfolio. this is a country which has enormous potential – and our readiness to engage with iran constructively has been made over and over. i shall continue to make that case. i sincerely hope that, during the time of my mandate, i will return to this house with a more positive picture of relations with iran.

high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy/vice-president of the commission. − madam president, we know the reason why yemen is on our agenda today. we traced the detroit bomber’s trail from the united states to europe, to africa and yemen. thus we were reminded, once again, that our own security is at risk if we do not help countries, like yemen, who are struggling to meet multiple challenges at the same time. terrorism is the immediate focus but is only one of an interlinked set of challenges. there is instability in the north, fuelled by armed conflict with the houthi rebels. there is conflict over land and water rights and longstanding tensions with the southern region, which has felt marginalised since unification in 1991. the government has so far been able to maintain overall stability but, as oil revenues have dwindled, the state is struggling to maintain control over parts of the national territory. to this we can add piracy in the gulf of aden, smuggling, migration and people-trafficking from the horn of africa and, now, a rise in jihadist terrorism. yemen has substantial population growth and an increasingly discontented young population. an inclusive internal political consensus on the way forward remains elusive. amidst all this one thing is clear: none of us can afford a zone of near-lawlessness stretching from the horn of africa to afghanistan. we would pay the price ourselves. over the last 18 months, the european union has highlighted yemen as a priority case in its counter-terrorism strategy and its comprehensive approach to state-building and development. the council adopted extensive conclusions on yemen in october. we are now seeking to rally all our key players around the strategy. the uk initiative to organise a high-level meeting with and on yemen next week could, therefore, not be more timely. a key focus of the meeting will be security. a significant package is now being prepared to help boost government efforts: training and equipment for law enforcement, a better legal framework and criminal justice system, work on anti-radicalisation and conflict prevention. this will come on top of eur 11 million allocated, in the commission’s development programme, to police training and juvenile justice in the last two years. the establishment of al-qa’ida in yemen is a symptom of deeper problems. the linkage between economic, political, social and security challenges are crucial. this is why we need a comprehensive approach. it is also vital that the yemeni state boosts its capacity to meet the needs of people throughout the country. the eu will propose to increase by one third its development funds foreseen for the period 2011-13. humanitarian aid from echo will continue in 2010. we continuously raise with the government the problems of access to the many displaced people. no amount of aid, however, can substitute for commitment and action by the government itself. president saleh’s stated commitment to national dialogue amongst all relevant actors has the potential to build a new national consensus, if all actors are included and their interests are taken into account. the international community should lend sustained support to this dialogue. it is the only sustainable way forward. last, but certainly not least, key regional players need to be engaged in the common effort to work with yemen – chief amongst these is saudi arabia. the london meeting offers an invaluable chance to include the saudis, the united states and others in a meaningful international dialogue on, and with, yemen. i look forward to our debates.

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european union is based on a relationship of solidarity between its member states. a clear example of this solidarity is administrative cooperation in tax matters, which is a key element in the functioning of the union. it is a question of loyalty between the member states, between their tax administrations; a loyalty which is translated into trust, into the confidence that the partners will also be allies and will not allow fraudsters to find refuge in their territory for their fraudulent activities. tax fraud pollutes the whole economy, has serious consequences for national budgets by reducing the capacity to bear expenditure and to carry out investments, leads to a breach of the principle of fiscal fairness vis-à-vis compliant citizens and leads to distortions of competition resulting in a poor functioning of the market. all these effects are all the more worrying because the volume of tax fraud in the european union is estimated to exceed €200 billion a year. this is twice the cost of the commission's proposed economic recovery plan, and it is therefore a very large sum. we are therefore faced with a major challenge which we must face with all our resolve, and although the directive currently in force was undoubtedly a first step in this direction, despite being full of good intentions, its practical application has not produced the desired effects. the time has come to take the next step and to equip ourselves with new instruments so that taxation can go hand in hand with market integration and liberalisation. i therefore welcome the proposal put forward by commissioner kovács and would like to congratulate him on his entire mandate and today, in particular, on this draft new directive. with this proposal we will have more and more effective means of combating tax fraud and tax evasion in europe. in this sense, the new directive represents a quantitatively and qualitatively significant leap forward: quantitatively, because it introduces new obligations, and qualitatively, because it extends and specifies those already envisaged. the scope of the objective is broadened from the exchange of information on request to automatic exchange. and finally, the third innovation: the lifting of banking secrecy. let me refer to this measure as the star of the proposal, because in practice such secrecy is the biggest obstacle for tax administrations. the lifting of banking secrecy has been an old claim of the oecd, reclaimed by the g-20. the commission's proposal is to be implemented in the next few years. this is the same objective pursued by the report we are examining today. it is our intention to intensify the results of the commission's proposal. the aim is to make the new directive more effective and more applicable. the commission has also proposed that the directive be amended to include the possibility of the exchange of information between the member states and the commission. there are also compromise amendments, namely those relating to the automatic exchange of information, data protection and confidentiality and the exchange of information with third countries. finally, i would like to thank my colleagues in the commission for their work and their spirit of collaboration and congratulate them on that. we have reached a broad consensus: the message from this parliament is clear and its firm commitment to the fight against tax fraud and evasion and to strengthening these great principles of the eu: loyalty, transparency and fair competition.

to increase tax cooperation are worthwhile. i am grateful for your support and for the work of the four rapporteurs, and i am very grateful for the support for these important commission initiatives. the rapporteur. - mr president, i would like to refer to the reasons why we are going beyond the standards set by the oecd in terms of automatic exchange of information. we could analyse many arguments, but it is clear that the oecd model is conceived in a broader framework for international relations, which responds to very different rules of the game from those of the european union. in the european union, we have the same economic space - as mr kovács has said - in which tax information must circulate as easily as taxable persons, so that each member state can apply its tax system. it is a single market in which there are no barriers to persons or goods and therefore there need not be any barriers to tax information. the member states are part of a political project and the relations between their tax systems must be in accordance with this political project. beyond the obvious practical imperative, we are faced with a question of principle. i would also like to stress the idea that fiscal sovereignty, in the fight against fraud, is strengthened rather than undermined. in other words, member states will have their fiscal sovereignty strengthened by having more effective instruments to implement their own tax systems. and so this is an issue that we must take into account and that is why we must support this directive. i would also like to stress that fraud, as mr klinz has said, is a criminal offence. we cannot justify this with such trivial arguments as the high taxation of the various tax systems. on the contrary, i would say that if we reduce tax evasion, we can reduce taxes. it is true that we must continue to work towards simplifying the various tax systems. and in conclusion, i would like to stress the important disincentive effect of the four reports and the four directives that we are supporting, in that when taxpayers are aware that thanks to this legislation there is less space and less refuge for those who cheat, the temptation to try to do so will be much less. and if they do, we will have more effective tools to prosecute such fraud. finally, i would like to stress the temporary value of this measure, since the crisis has shown the danger of opacity, the contagion from one country to another and the need for public stimulus. i would like to refer here to the support of mr lamberts, who points out that we are at a time when public finances must make a special effort to adopt measures of economic recovery and social protection to cushion the effects of the crisis. the citizens are therefore more aware than ever of the seriousness of tax fraud and its effects on the economy as a whole, and they are demanding that their representatives take appropriate measures to combat it.

the determination of their legal status fall within the sole responsibility and competence of a receiving eu member state or schengen-associated country. former detainees received under this scheme may have access to rehabilitation measures in the eu member states under the applicable national laws. in the context of the abovementioned statement on the closure of guantánamo, on 16 june 2009 the president of the council wrote to the co-chairman of the us detention policy task force. in this letter the european union put forward a non-paper with principles of international law relevant to the fight against terrorism. it includes unequivocal statements on due process guarantees, such as access to court to challenge arrest, detention and transfer, as well as on the prohibition of torture. they have been discussed in detail in the dialogue on counter-terrorism and international law. the commission considers these guarantees to be important to this dialogue, as they contribute to a better understanding of how the fight against terrorism should respect the rule of law and international law, including international human rights law, international refugee law and international humanitarian law. as already mentioned, the european union opposes the death penalty and has intervened in individual cases with third countries, including the united states, to prevent it from being carried out. the commission will consider appropriate steps in case the death penalty is imposed on a former guantánamo detainee tried by a us court or military commission. the european commission appreciates the steps taken so far by president obama to close guantánamo and hopes to see further progress on this in the future.

mr president, i would ask the spanish presidency to preserve bluefin tuna, but also to preserve the traditional art of fishing for mediterranean cod. this art, which has coexisted with the bluefin for over a thousand years, has never endangered it. what really endangers bluefin tuna is illegal fishing, industrial fishing, fencing and the proliferation of farms. this is the real problem with bluefin tuna. we should not be unfair: we should be able to distinguish between what is really endangering bluefin tuna, which is this type of industrial fishing - fencing - and traditional fishing. the policy must be fair and therefore we should look for a way of actually preserving tuna, but, of course, without punishing these traditional arts. i believe that there is a perfect balance, sometimes impossible to achieve, but we must try to find that way to effectively preserve this species, to ensure that it does not go extinct, without punishing traditional mediterranean arts such as the mattress.
mr president, i share the concern about the biological situation of the bluefin tuna stock and agree with the need for effective conservation and management measures which not only prevent its collapse but also ensure the sustainability of fisheries and responsible trade. my country has been working in this direction for years. in addition to the age-old example of the almadraba, it has created a protection zone in the mediterranean, limited the fencing fleet to six vessels and pioneered the adoption of a recovery plan for the species and documented control of trade. including bluefin tuna in appendix 1 to cites would lead to the prohibition of international trade in bluefin tuna without addressing the underlying problems: it does not limit the volume of catches, it can divert flags towards consumer countries and it is a step outside the recent agreements of iccat, the regional fisheries management organisation responsible for the management of this fishery, and would therefore weaken the international governance of the seas and the principle of responsible fishing. we have to get to the root of the problem. we support the reduction of catches already agreed at iccat and even a moratorium if the scientific reports in progress for the next season so determine. we want the european union to strengthen its control deployment and to comply with the iccat recommendations to ensure the traceability of catching processes and trade. this line of action is compatible with the inclusion of bluefin tuna in cites appendix 2, but is not compatible with appendix 1, which should be reserved for a different scenario and not subject to conditions that would erode its own credibility as a cites instrument. in any event, this debate should send a clear message: the european union is fully committed to the sustainability of bluefin tuna and will take the necessary measures to preserve it. the industry must show that quotas work and are enforced and that illegal fishing can be controlled. to save the fish, we must save the species.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, bluefin tuna has been on red alert for some time, and we have been hearing reports for years clearly demonstrating the weakness of the stock and how we have contributed to that weakness of the stock, including through public subsidies. in the european union we have been paying as much as 34 million euros for modernisation in recent years. i think it is necessary for us to say this, to take responsibility for the situation we are in. we have brought the bluefin tuna stock to the brink of collapse and now we cannot say that we have no responsibility. today we have the opportunity to correct this problem by including bluefin tuna in appendix i of cites, and only then can we do so because, i repeat, there are many people who live off it. it is true that there are sectors which have done things well and which can and should continue to do things well, but in order for them to do things well there must be tuna. without tuna, they can't do anything at all. the only guarantee that this will be fulfilled is appendix i and therefore any other measure which can clearly distort that proposal is a bad measure which will, in any case, prolong the agony but will not end that agony. so let's not get confused, let's not cheat, we have a historical responsibility to the species and to the people and families who live off that. we are taking our responsibility with courage and with the honour that the european union deserves at this time.
mr president, with regard to the possible ban on bluefin tuna fishing in the mediterranean, i am very much afraid that legal fishing will be replaced by illegal fishing and that the just will pay for the wicked. in catalonia, hundreds of jobs are at stake. there is a respectful fishery, fully regulated and controlled, both in fisheries management and commercial management. since 2006, the bluefin tuna fishery in the eastern atlantic and the mediterranean has been reduced from 30 000 tonnes to 13 500 tonnes. the minimum size of fish has been increased from 10 to 30 kilograms, and from 11 months of fishing to 11 months of sealing. finally, i think there is no consensus among international experts on the danger of extinction of bluefin tuna. if you compare stocks between 1970 and 2010, which is when control data is available, the bluefin tuna population would be above 15%, between 21 and 30%, therefore clearly above 15% of cites appendix 1.
mr president, i also want to speak about commercial fisheries and to make it very clear that it is the regional fisheries organisations that are already involved in the management and conservation of these species. in fact, a simple reading of the cites convention will tell you that it may be intended for elephants and polar bears, but it is certainly not intended for commercial fisheries. i am not against the protection of bluefin tuna, because it would be absurd, if only because of its importance to the fleet, but i believe that measures should be taken by the bodies which have the best specialists in both fisheries management and scientific research, because cites has to have recourse to external advice when it receives proposals on these species. i therefore consider the proposal to include bluefin tuna in appendix i of cites to be unnecessary and unjustified, because it already has the measures imposed by iccat, unfair, because it would harm a fleet that has just embarked on a huge effort to reduce fishing, and even counterproductive, because it can give rise to an uncontrollable black market in bluefin tuna. i understand the enormous pressure which environmental ngos are putting on public opinion in general and this house in particular, as is being seen, and that is why my group has decided to support inclusion in appendix ii as a compromise between the environment committee's proposal and those of us who think that fisheries management cannot be taken away from regional fisheries organisations. and our proposal is based on the scientific advice of cites. the fao has recommended the inclusion of bluefin tuna in appendix ii of cites exclusively, which shows that many have not even read the fao report.
mr president, we have heard today that illegal fishing is being mixed with the mafia, and i too want to speak out in favour of a sector which has shown itself to be responsible on many occasions. i am in favour of the need to control fisheries. i also support the need to control the mafia. but this cannot be a reason to include bluefin tuna in appendix i. i should also like to say that the basque fleet, which will be very much affected by this decision if it is adopted, has shown itself to be responsible, because in order to defend the sector, it has on occasion even requested the suspension of fishing for anchovy, for example. i must also say that we must listen to what iccat said, which adopted in 2009 more restrictive and stronger management measures in line with the recommendations of the scientific committee. i would remind you that a percentage of 3 500 tonnes of fishing quota has been set for 2010. in 2009 it was 22 000 tonnes, and in 2006 32 000. and so the commitment was also made to take further control measures if necessary. i am not in favour of the inclusion of bluefin tuna in this appendix i; it can harm many sectors, including the artisanal sector which has not been taken into account today. we should therefore only support their inclusion on the assumption that these measures would not be effective.

member of the commission. − mr president, first of all, with respect to the procedure – because a lot of questions have been asked about that – obviously, this will be the first time that parliament has had to give its consent on the agreement as such and also the first time that the safeguard clauses will have to be adopted by codecision. this has consequences, i think, for the relationship between the council, the commission and parliament. the safeguard clauses are a proposal. the commission adopted its proposal yesterday and it will be presented to the council and parliament very soon. obviously, then, it will be a codecision procedure, so i do not understand the many remarks in which you put questions and express doubts about safeguard clauses. there will only be safeguard clauses that get your agreement, because it is codecision: it is as simple as that. so you should not be so worried about it and about ratification by parliament. that implies, of course, that there will be a debate in your committee. i already said during the hearing that i am not going to make a proposal for an early, provisional application unless parliament has itself pronounced on the agreement, whether as formal ratification by parliament or by some other procedure that we can establish between the inta committee and the commission. that remains open and can be discussed, but in any case parliament will have the opportunity to give its political judgement on the agreement before any proposals for early application are put forward. another question is whether this is a mixed agreement or an agreement which is only about community competences. the legal service is still preparing an opinion on that, but we cannot rule out the possibility that in the end we will have to consider this a mixed agreement, which implies that all the national parliaments will also have to ratify it, and which could also have – in reply to niccolò rinaldi’s question – consequences for the voting procedure in council. so much for the procedure: you will have every opportunity to express yourselves, and we will scrupulously respect this – if we did not do so i think we would get into mr president, i would like to denounce the situation of the catalan and european swine sector. the price of pigs has continued to decrease for over a year and for several months now has been clearly below the production cost. one of the reasons why it is happening is because of pig imports from emerging countries. in too many cases these imports enter the european union without being sufficiently controlled at european customs. in too many cases, these pig imports do not fulfil several european regulations on quality and food security that the european union imposes only on european producers. it seems that the same will happen in the coming years: increasing animal welfare requirements for european producers but with no controls on imports from emerging countries. this is a clear case of unfair competition. in this way europe will lose its farmers and pig producers and, without them, europe will lose an important part of its agri-food industry. these worries i wanted to share with you.

the next item is the report by mrs maria do céu patrão neves, on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on the green paper on the reform of the common fisheries policy (com (2009) 0163 - 2009/2106 (ini)) (a7-0014/2010).
on behalf of the s&d group. thank you, mr. martin fragueiro, and welcome, and thank you, mrs. damanaki. i too am opening today on the subject of fisheries and we are facing a major challenge. we are obliged to define responsibly the guidelines that will guarantee the sustainability of the seas, of fisheries and, ultimately, of the planet itself. we are also talking about an important productive fabric that affects our countries, our coasts, our regions - an economic and cultural fabric with many values - and, as you have very well said, mrs damanaki, there are problems with the 2002 reform. we must review the principle of relative stability, we must look for new management formulas which are more flexible, more adaptable, because the issue of tacs and quotas has been problematic. they have had problems with the famous issue of discards, discards that neither the fishermen nor the planet itself can afford. the future reform of the cfp must ensure a sustainable fisheries system and we call for a new management system based on fishing effort. we have to open up, we have to think and we have to try to make the management situation more flexible. we must introduce, to a large extent, environmental criteria, the differentiation between bottom fishing and high-altitude fishing. it's important, it's something the whole sector is demanding. we must reduce the overcapacity of some fleets. the common organization of the market, the question of stabilizing the market and how to reconcile it with the import of fish from third countries remain unresolved. the fight against illegal fishing, which has been denounced and has so far been ineffective, needs more means, more resources, unification of sanctions, international agreements based on principles of legality, on principles of human rights, on principles of compliance with agreements. a financial framework, which you have said must be more effective, must be more effective than current policy. and above all, the social factor: we are talking about people, we must give them dignity, give them a professionalism, give them a professional recognition, give them an economic capacity to survive. and, of course, the integration of women, that invisible part that has never been seen in the fishing world. we must make it clear and we must make an effort to do so. reform of the fisheries policy is more than just making legislation. it is addressing an important part of the reform, from the european union, that will ensure the sustainability of the seas, of fishermen and of part of the world. so we have to be brave in the face of challenges, and to be brave is to face politics without fear. and the fears, of course, we have to let go. we must look at the situation head on and maintain the balance of the state itself, the european union itself and the world itself.
mr president, we are risking everything in this reform. if we do not act now, there will be no more opportunities to create a real fisheries policy and we will be partly responsible for the failure. the cfp has been subject to increasingly justified criticism for years and it is discouraging that, when we are given a last chance, this parliament is not able to propose alternatives to what we have so often criticised and, in particular, to the obvious failure, both because of the state of the resources and the decline of the sector, of a conservation and management system. it is incomprehensible that they are afraid to suggest clearly alternatives to those already discussed in this house in 1996, such as transferable quota systems or effort management, which have produced such good results and could help to maintain at least the most industrial fleets. the report says that there cannot be a one-size-fits-all solution, but at the same time it excludes the possibility of different solutions. i do not understand the contradiction, nor do i understand that if someone does not want to use an instrument, the solution is to ban it for everyone. this is not protection of the weakest, it is fear on the part of certain sectors who see only solutions in permanent subsidies. the cfp should also be a guarantee of competitiveness in a globalised world of fisheries products, whose market will undoubtedly continue to grow, but without us, it seems. the community's policies should be coherent and we cannot allow trade policy and rules of origin such as those resulting from the new economic association agreements to destroy the competitiveness of community fisheries without providing third countries with nothing but mere gestures, at the expense of our fishing industry. mr president, consensus is good when it is achieved to move forward, not at the expense of standing still in the face of problems, and we have many problems to solve.
mr barreiro, mrs damanaki, we need clear objectives, courage and to avoid another failure; the key to this is participation. the extractive sector and the processing industry are the first stakeholders in the sustainability of fisheries, which is why their involvement in the design of the reform or their participation, as in 2009, in the revision of a control regulation, which should have been drawn up in a more open way, is basic to meet the objectives of the reform: to have a sustainable and profitable sector and to guarantee supply. the other keywords are: regionalization, responsibility, stability and justice. regionalization, to take account of the specificities of each area and type of fishing, separating artisanal from industrial; responsibility, giving priority to good practices and efforts to reduce fishing capacity already made; stability, through long-term management plans based on increasingly sound scientific activity; and justice, by revising the sector's cmo and offering inspection and control activities by third countries to encourage sustainable behaviour in the sector. and justice, too, for the women of the sea, forever forgotten in this sector; without their work, fishing, in many parts of the world, would be impossible.
mr president, the reform of the common fisheries policy plays an important part in the future of europe. the fisheries sector is a means and a way of life in our coastal areas, the basis of our canning industry and marine research. it is fundamental to the safety, quality and price of the food supply to our consumers. it is also for foreign relations and development. the reform must be geared towards responsible, sustainable and competitive fishing. it must emphasise its social dimension, have an ecosystem approach and be integrated into marine policy. the conservation and recovery of resources must be ensured and the principle of relative stability must be reviewed. the management policy based on tacs and quotas should be open to the management of fishing effort. we must increase control and eradicate unfair competition. the small-scale fishing fleet and areas highly dependent on fishing need differentiated treatment and greater socioeconomic support. the shellfish sector must be fully integrated into the common fisheries policy. i support the report and congratulate the rapporteur and the co-rapporteurs on the commitments they have made. i ask the commission and the council presidency to take this very seriously in their future work.
mr president, i too would like to take this opportunity to stress the points which some of us believe should be central to the outcome of the report we are about to vote on. i would remind you of some of these points: the precautionary principle, which is fundamental and essential; capacity reduction, which is absolutely essential; limitation of public subsidy policy; improvement of the control and prosecution of crime, without respite and with clear consequences for those who do wrong and encourage others to do wrong; but at the same time, we must promote sustainable arts and crafts, sustainable fishing, which necessarily implies making progress in defining what we mean by artisanal fishing, which indeed needs greater concreteness. i would also like to mention the role of women and the recognition we owe to their work, on which we have also tabled amendments. finally, i think it is important to stress and call for greater coherence and responsibility in fisheries agreements with third countries; those concluded with morocco and guinea, for example, oblige us to do so.
acting president of the council. - mr president, i too would like to thank mrs patrão neves for her work. so far, as regards the discussions that have taken place in the council, i must say that the ministers have unanimously supported the need for reform, consisting in simplifying the rules, in strengthening the role of the regional level and in decentralising decision-making, except for the strategic elements and principles, and they agree that discards, overcapacity and overfishing must be reduced. the specific points of convergence so far are: the maintenance of the current rules for access to the 12-mile zone, long-term management of resources, greater partnership between fishermen, market incentives - such as labelling and certificates - to stimulate the share of fishermen's overall income, the use of subsidies only as exceptional measures to reduce excess capacity, the importance of research in fisheries policy, the integration of aquaculture, the relationship of the cfp with the integrated maritime policy and the need to maintain and increase the european union's action at international level. the discussions so far have also revealed divergent positions on the following issues: relative stability, the current system of tacs and quotas and the use of transferable quotas, effort limitation as a management tool, methods to reduce discards, overcapacity and overfishing, and global financing and its allocation, as well as increased support for small-scale fishing and coastal communities. as i said at the beginning of my speech, the council has not yet adopted a position; it is not planned to take formal decisions until next year, when the commission has formally presented the legislative proposals. and finally, i would also like to welcome the fisheries sector, which is present here in this chamber today.

mr president, commissioner, the crisis has shown that the european union has no instruments to counteract its effects and to steer economic recovery in the right direction. it is therefore necessary to formulate a common response based, in addition to the coordination of member states' strategies, on the european union's own instruments, which give it a real capacity to act in order to provide an immediate and comprehensive response. the first objective should be to provide the union with greater and better economic governance and, to this end, greater financial autonomy. in this context, a financial transaction tax designed to fulfil a triple function is of great interest, because it is necessary to strengthen the european union's capacity to develop its own policies; because it is necessary to provide greater stability to the economy by curbing speculative operations; because it is necessary to provide the information needed to monitor the evolution and situation of financial markets; and also because, in designing this tax figure, the financial sector should be sought to contribute to repairing the damage in the real economy and to covering the expenses and costs of stabilising the banking system. commissioner, can you give us a calendar?

mr president, the 2008 competition policy report introduces a chapter on cartels and consumers, reports on the imposition of coercive fines for the first time, and includes important initiatives such as the guidelines accompanying the energy package and a white paper on actions for damages for infringement of competition rules. it addresses the role of competition policy in the crisis, the effects of which have helped to stabilise and mitigate state aid. in the pending exit process, the distortions caused must be corrected and a level playing field restored, avoiding moral hazard. this report calls for a horizon for the automobile sector, attention to the problems of smes and an investigation of the food chain with follow-up measures for dairy products. it also advocates a more sophisticated and legitimate competition policy, reinforcing the role of parliament. that is why we support it and i congratulate the rapporteur on the result achieved.

in writing. - i voted in favour of this important report because it supports the commission's proposal to extend the transitional regime for rabies, bringing it to an end in a way that better coincides with the period when the european commission expects to conclude community financing of vaccination programmes aimed at eradicating wild rabies, the main rabies problem in the eu, in some member states. in addition, the commission has adopted a prudent precautionary approach, which emphasises prevention and additional health considerations related to the internal market and the free movement of pet animals. the commission has compared and examined the different policy options, taking into account the different opinions of the european food safety authority (efsa). the proposed date for the end of the transitional arrangements will allow for the conversion of infrastructures and gradual vocational retraining as well as the adaptation of the on-site staff to the new situation.
in writing. − i voted, together with my group, in favour of this report because it points out that the proposals made in this framework seek to make it easier for third-country nationals legally residing in a member state to move in the schengen area on the basis of a d long-stay visa issued by that member state. they are intended to provide a response to situations where member states are unable, for various reasons, to issue residence permits in time to third-country nationals residing in their territory, by extending the existing principle of equivalence between a residence permit and short-stay c visas to long-stay d visas. a long-stay visa will thus have the same effect as a residence permit as regards circulation in the schengen area. this will make it possible for anyone in possession of a document showing that he is legally resident in a member state to move freely in the schengen area for short periods of no more than three months in any half year.

position. this is also the rationale that has led numerous member states to resume their development cooperation with cuba over the past few months, representing a diverse range of the political believe that the way forward is to pursue and deepen the ongoing political dialogue and continue cooperation with cuba as a tool for improving the lives of the cuban people. cooperation with cuba has never been suspended by the european union, because development is not about supporting the government – it is about supporting the people. our view has always been that development cooperation reconstruction after the hurricanes, food security and adaptation to climate change. projects are also being run in support of non-state actor activities. i would like to be very clear that there is union in cuba. it is important that the european union continues to address the basic needs of the cuban population while intervening in strategic sectors through the available thematic or geographical instruments. the task that the eu needs to face in a determined way is to find the right balance between showing openness to dialogue, supporting the cuban population through development cooperation and reaffirming our principles.

acting president of the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to begin by stressing the importance of the strategic energy plan and its necessary contribution to accelerating the development and application of clean, sustainable and efficient energy technologies. without this plan, it will not be possible to achieve the 2020 targets we have set ourselves, nor to achieve the transition to a low-carbon economy of the desired size by 2050. i am glad to see that there is a broad agreement between parliament and the council on the importance and necessity of both the objectives of the plan and the means to be made available to it. the energy council intends to adopt conclusions on the eete plan at its meeting on friday 12 march. these will be an important reference for the spring european council on 25 march, as the issue of climate change is on its agenda. the proposal for conclusions to be discussed in the council incorporates the subject of financing, albeit in a duly cautious manner. we do not want to prejudge the negotiations that will have to be carried out on this subject in the context of the next financial framework. the main points in this proposal for a conclusion are as follows. firstly, the time has come to move from the technological roadmaps to the operational launching of european industrial initiatives. we must do it step by step, but as quickly as possible. secondly, the way forward for future energy research cooperation in europe must be through the effective use of public resources and the creation of flexible public-private partnerships with industry. the commission is therefore invited to establish a platform that includes all the financial organisations concerned, so that they can exchange information and best practice, while, where appropriate, coordinating their actions as necessary. third, given the scale of public-private financing needed in the medium term to support, in particular, large demonstration projects, an increase in the share of public investment at eu level may be necessary. this is a matter which must be taken into account both in the review of the budget and in the negotiations for the next financial framework. fourthly, the authorities in the member states should be encouraged and supported to provide appropriate incentives and give consistent signals to put this policy into action. if necessary, they should also significantly increase public funding for the development of low-carbon technologies. fifthly, the commission and the european investment bank are already working together to improve the coordination and continuity of the financing of demonstration projects in the energy sector with high technological risk. they are also working to mobilise and make available other sources of funding, both public and private. finally, the commission and the european investment bank are trying to assess the optimal financing packages for large demonstration projects, and the commission is therefore also invited to examine new ways of combining resources from different sources and to develop an ad hoc instrument for financing the commercial launch of low-carbon technologies. ladies and gentlemen, all of this sends a clear message about future investment in the development of low-carbon technologies. despite the heavy budgetary constraints at present, the message that the council will send at its meeting this friday will be a message of commitment, a positive message in terms both of the importance of this issue at european level and of the enormous value of each member state investing in the development of low-carbon technologies.
member of the commission. − madam president, although i am replacing my colleague günther oettinger today, it is a real pleasure to discuss with you the future of low-carbon technologies. i personally was closely involved in the development of the european strategic energy technology plan (set plan) in the last commission and i believe strongly that the development of these technologies is one of the cornerstones of the energy policy we have to develop jointly in the years to come. parliament’s report on the set plan of june 2008 was very clear in proposing an appropriate level of ambition. we should not now lower this ambition. today you have asked three clear questions and i will respond to them in turn. first, regarding our priorities for 2010 to 2020 and the launch of the european industrial initiatives, those six initiatives really match our priorities – wind, solar bio-energy, sustainable fission, smart grids, and carbon capture and storage are priorities that were strongly endorsed by parliament and the council. at your request, we have also prioritised energy efficiency by developing a new dedicated initiative – ‘smart cities’ – to unlock the market potential of energy efficient technologies in cities and regions. to prioritise activities within this initiative, the commission has developed, together with the stakeholders, technology road maps for the period 2010-2020. these road maps establish concrete objectives as well as the activities needed to achieve them. the initiatives are mature for launching this year, 2010. smart cities are planned for the following year. your second question concerns the need for predictable, stable and adequate budgets for the set plan in the current financing period and post-2014. our estimate of the public and private investment needs for the development of low-carbon technologies in the set plan is eur 8 billion per year. today about eur 3 billion are being invested annually in the european union, which means that a further eur 50 billion is needed for the period 2010-2020. bridging this gap should be one of the key institutional discussions over the coming years. effort must be focused where intervention is most efficient, avoiding duplications and fostering the greatest potential impact in the market. it is clear that eu level investments – coming either from the seventh framework programme or the european energy programme for recovery – will not be enough. nor will the potential funds from the 300 million emissions trading allowances set aside for the demonstration of carbon capture and storage and innovative renewable technologies. at current prices this is approximately eur 4 billion. major efforts are therefore required, both by the private and public sector; the public sector includes both the european union and of course also the member states. to be blunt, the bulk of the money will have to come from where the bulk of the money is. thirdly, you asked if the commission intends to finance other technology avenues and propose additional industrial initiatives. other technologies that deserve european-level intervention will certainly emerge over time, so the set plan must remain flexible, as we have already shown with the new initiative on energy efficiency – smart cities – which we expect to launch, as i said, in 2011. we will closely monitor the most promising technologies through the set plan information system. setis, as this is called, is already working on storage and ocean technologies to assess their potential and identify the best opportunities for european intervention. we have also encouraged the establishment of a new technology platform on renewables, heating and cooling, that should help the sectors involved better to define their technology transfer. i am very pleased to see this file getting the support it deserves. it is a key file for achieving our energy policy goals, a key file for europe and for our future.
the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment is a very important one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done. several studies estimate that promoting the 20% renewable energy penetration target will result in 2.8 million european workers being employed in this sector by 2020. in addition, it is estimated that two thirds of the jobs created will come from small and medium-sized enterprises. and the key, ladies and gentlemen, is in the development of green technologies. in order to achieve this, my group advocates three main objectives. firstly, a real commitment to provide new funds for the eete plan. it's not enough to regroup and rename the support programs we already have. we agree that our objective must be translated into a clear increase in the appropriations for research into renewable energy and energy efficiency. we need to do so now, at the next review of the financial perspectives and, of course, when negotiating the new ones. secondly, if we are to create the jobs our economy needs to get out of the crisis, it is vital that we push forward the demonstration phase of innovative technologies and we must facilitate their market uptake. and finally, we cannot harness the potential for green job creation if we do not have a highly skilled workforce. we need to invest in education and information to strengthen the links between the world of work and the world of education, and we need to foster skills of excellence in r & d and innovation to be in a position to fill the potential gaps in the renewable energy labour market.
member of the commission. − madam president, only two weeks after the dreadful disaster on madeira, the commission was again shocked and saddened by the death and devastation caused by storm xynthia in france and other european countries. i wish to express my personal sympathy to all those that are suffering as a consequence of the disaster. the commission’s condolences go in particular to the families and friends of those that have lost their lives. through the monitoring and information centre for civil protection, the commission has been monitoring the events caused by storm xynthia closely and has offered to set the mechanism for eu assistance in action. fortunately, the french rescue services were able to respond to the disaster with their own means and did not request the activation of the mechanism. together with the relevant authorities in the member states, the commission is now exploring all the possibilities and instruments that could be available at eu level to assist financially in overcoming the disaster and to help return to normal living conditions as soon as possible. two days ago commission president barroso met french president sarkozy to discuss the situation. yesterday he also met with a number of members of this house from different countries. one week ago my colleague, mr hahn, commissioner responsible for regional policy and the solidarity fund, visited the most hard-hit regions in france – la rochelle and l’aiguillon-sur-mer – and met with national and regional authorities. on madeira, where disaster struck two weeks earlier, the authorities and rescue services have been able to make enormous progress in combating the effects of the flooding disaster. commissioner hahn visited madeira during the past weekend to get a first-hand impression and to discuss with the local authorities the way forward. the european union solidarity fund was set up in 2002 specifically as the instrument at eu level to financially assist eu member states affected by major natural disasters, if certain conditions are met. france has already declared its intention to apply for assistance from the solidarity fund. i should point out that the regulation governing the solidarity fund normally allows its mobilisation only for what are known as ‘major disasters’, where the damage at national level exceeds the threshold of 0.6% of gross national income, or eur 3 billion at 2002 prices. for france this currently means the damage would have to exceed approximately eur 3.4747 billion at current prices. however, in exceptional circumstances and if specific criteria are met, the fund may also be used for smaller ‘extraordinary regional disasters’, in particular where they concern outermost regions like madeira. the french authorities are currently carrying out an assessment of the damage and of its repercussions for the economy and the living conditions of the population. these are the essential elements for the application, which has to reach the commission within 10 weeks of the disaster. that means before 9 may. after it is received it will be examined by the commission as quickly as possible. the commission services, in particular dg regional policy, are granting all possible assistance and guidance in preparing the application. contacts at expert level are well established with the french authorities, thus allowing effective progress. please be aware, however, that aid from the solidarity fund cannot be paid out immediately. the solidarity fund should not be misunderstood as an emergency instrument. it is a financial instrument to help bear the financial burden of emergency operations. as such, a possible grant could be used retroactively for emergency operations from day one of the disaster. the funding for the solidarity fund is raised through an extra effort of the member states outside the normal european union budget. it has to be approved by parliament and the council through an amending budget procedure. as you know, the whole procedure – from the moment the application is made to paying out the grant – inevitably takes several months. the commission is, however, making every effort to keep this time span as short as possible. as regards the structural funds, in particular the erdf, this can of course not be used for immediate emergency operations. france and the commission have, however, started discussing the options and possible necessary programme modifications which might be instrumental for longer-term reconstruction and for investment in businesses affected by the flood. one last point, which members of this house already raised during the debate on madeira two weeks ago. the commission will use the current political momentum to attempt to unblock the proposal for an amended solidarity fund regulation at the council. parliament widely supported this proposal, and i feel this is the right moment to take common action vis-à-vis the council again.

acting president of the council. - mr president, i thank the european parliament for taking the initiative in holding this debate on what i consider to be one of the most important, most relevant from a democratic point of view, aspects of the development of the european union and of europeanism among the citizens of the european union. this is a very important issue, which opens up a new stage in the european union; as you know, of course, it is a question of the citizens' initiative. in other words, the possibility of at least one million european citizens from different countries being able to sign a legislative initiative. the commission is the community body with the power to initiate legislation. the citizens' initiative is a very clear priority of the council presidency. very clear. it is a priority because we understand that it is a priority for europe. when a country holds the presidency of the council of the european union, we understand that it does not have to develop its priorities, its objectives as a country, but that it must go further and be able to represent the objectives of europe. citizens' initiative, with its possibilities, with the rights it gives to citizens - to the almost 500 million european citizens - is an essential objective of europe and is therefore one of the priorities of the spanish presidency; not because it is a priority for spain, but because it is a priority for europe. citizens are hoping that the treaty of lisbon will be developed as quickly as possible after eight years of wasting time in institutional uncertainties. we must make up for lost time and give an answer to the citizens, who want to participate. that is to say, to strike a balance between the europe that has been built up during the 20th century from the top down - albeit a democratic europe - and a europe that is also built from the bottom up. we therefore believe that the citizens' initiative should be launched as soon as possible, because it will be a test of the political will of governments, the european parliament and the union's institutions to give citizens a voice and a capacity to participate in the life of the union. in addition, to counteract something that unfortunately happens in the european union, namely that the political debate is, for the most part, a national debate, an in-house debate. here in brussels, or in this parliament, a european debate is taking place, but in each of the countries of the union the national debate predominates, not the european debate. the citizens' initiative is a formidable mechanism for triggering a genuine european debate from civil society. the initiatives put forward by citizens from different countries will trigger a european debate in each of the countries, not just a purely national debate. that is why we have considered the citizens' initiative a priority. as soon as the commission presents its draft regulation, we shall have a text so that, together with the council and the european parliament, we can have in place before the end of this semester what the european citizens are undoubtedly waiting for. we must work on the various aspects of the present situation, some of them more technical, others more political, but we must make sure that this happens. that is why we, from the informal meeting of ministers for european affairs at la granja in san ildefonso, which will recall mr šefčovič and mrs malmström - still in office because the new commission had not yet taken office - to the first meeting we had with the commission in madrid when the new college of commissioners took office and now this afternoon here in the european parliament, have that interest in pushing this initiative forward. i would ask you - and this is the message i would like to convey to you, ladies and gentlemen - to show the utmost interest in this initiative. i know they do. and they want to see the greatest possible speed with which something is being done which i think will be able to reach general agreement on its various aspects with some ease, because of the discussions which have taken place in the council with the commission and the european parliament. for example, in the committee i was on, the committee on institutional affairs. i therefore believe that we can put this into practice, which is undoubtedly one of the most exciting elements for citizens in the new stage which is now opening up in the european union.
member of the commission. − mr president, i would really like to thank parliament for putting this very important item on the agenda. i would like to personally thank my dear friend diego lópez garrido and the spanish presidency for keeping this on top of the spanish presidency’s agenda, because i believe that the instrument we are going to have will really change the way we do politics in the european union. until now, the european construct was based on representative democracy. i think this was very well reflected also in the lisbon treaty, where it is very clear that parliament’s powers are very much strengthened and when we are going to include the national parliaments more in the european legislative process. and we needed to complement it with greater inclusion of citizens in this process, through this instrument of participatory democracy. there was the debate, a while ago, on whether one cancels out the other and whether it is a zero-sum game. i really do not think so because i consider both elements of representative and participatory democracy as mutually reinforcing, and both help to create real european political and public space. i also believe that, thanks to this instrument, we will underline even more the importance of european citizenship for europeans. as diego has already said, i am also convinced that this would lead to stronger, better cross-border europe-wide debates in europe, more on european topics and not only on national topics that we see so often in the capitals of our member states. the commission was and is very grateful for the work the european parliament has already done on the european citizens’ initiative. for us, the resolution you adopted on 7 may last year was very important political guidance and a very important pointer as to how we should prepare this initiative. as you know, the commission, when preparing such important pieces of legislation like this one, wants to engage the european public in as wide a discussion as possible. therefore we organised a public debate on this issue, based on the green paper that we issued in december last year. i must say that we have been very positively surprised by the responses we have got. we got more than 300 responses coming from a range of contributors: individual citizens, organisations, public authorities and even some national parliaments. we evaluated the responses we got and completed the consultation process with a public debate in brussels, where more than 150 stakeholders were in attendance, including honourable representatives of parliament. if i had to sum up this debate, i would say that there were a lot of innovative, interesting and positive suggestions coming to the commission’s table. what were the major conclusions? that citizens are very much interested in having this initiative in place as soon as possible, that they would like to have it as user-friendly as possible, that they would like to have it simple, straightforward, understandable and, most of all, accessible. and, as you would agree, these are clear and very important parameters for having this legislation prepared in this way, because only these parameters would guarantee that citizens would use this instrument for better communication with the commission and with the european institutions. drawing on the results of the consultations and also on the proposals made by the european parliament, the commission is currently finalising its proposal. i hope that the college will adopt the proposals we are working on on 31 march. i can also tell you that this probably would not be possible without strong encouragement from the spanish presidency. it is very clear that such a top priority for the presidency must be respected, and i know there is strong member of the commission. − mr president, the members have for their consideration a draft decision supplementing the schengen borders code as regards the surveillance of the external borders in the context of frontex operations at sea. this is a necessary decision and it will help member states and frontex to manage our external sea borders more efficiently. as you know, the number of boats will increase very soon as they always do at this time of year in the mediterranean. the proposal contains a set of very important principles and clarifications of rules that border guards must apply when controlling sea borders, for example the principle of non-refoulement and the obligation to treat vulnerable peoples and unaccompanied minors with special care. it also clarifies what assistance should be provided to persons in danger at sea and where to disembark persons that are rescued. many of you in this house have asked for these principles and rules for years and now finally they are within our reach. the changes that we are proposing will also reduce the risk of lives being lost in the mediterranean by making sea border operations more efficient. the draft decision is the result of very hard and long discussions with member states and with experts from, for instance, the united nations high commissioner for refugees and the international organisation for migration. it will provide our institutions with a better framework for exercising a proper monitoring of these operations where significant european funds are involved. on the legal aspects of the proposal, the commission has chosen article 12 of the schengen border code as the legal basis because the rules concern border surveillance patrols during frontex operations, not border checks as i think parliament’s legal opinion argues. at the request of members of this house, the commission has made an investigation of alternative technical solutions that would allow for, firstly, not reopening the discussions on the substance and, secondly, having clear rules adopted in time for frontex operations this summer. unfortunately, we have not found such an alternative so i therefore recommend the honourable members not to reject these long-awaited new rules.

mr president, mr president of the european council, two messages: one of concern, the other of demanding encouragement for the work ahead. concern about the weak nature and genuine european dimension of the response, the involvement of the imf and the use of bilateral loans. concern about the ineffectiveness of the response, which means that in the short term the greek debt will become more expensive, but also concern about the lack of understanding of the underlying problem, which we have stressed here in this parliament. the greek problem is a problem for the euro area and, by extension, for the whole of the european union: the deficit and, consequently, the debt have soared as a result of the financial rescue plans, which have cost a lot, and therefore austerity should not jeopardise the investment needed for economic recovery, nor the financing of the reforms that are essential. that is why the second message is one of demanding encouragement. the necessary reforms must be accompanied by a strategy whose importance must not be diminished in the eyes of the europeans. let us therefore focus on the renewal of the european model that is so important to us: education, yes, and the knowledge society, but also a commitment to quality employment and above all to equal employment that will make us better off in the future without neglecting the fight against poverty. that is why i invite you, mr president of the european council, to make sure that the council and the commission, in the 2020 strategy which this parliament will also have to deal with, are ambitious and live up to their responsibilities, because it is clear that this parliament will, in any case, live up to its responsibilities in front of the european citizens who are watching us.
mr president, i will try to say two new things about two of the subjects discussed at the european council: strategy 2020 and the regulation of financial markets. with regard to strategy 2020, we have all said here for a long time that one of the reasons for the relative failure of the lisbon strategy was that there were not enough tools to force member states to honour their commitments. the commission and the european council are now coming up with a proposal which is more of the same: soft coordination, with reference to articles 121 and 136 of the treaty. the president-in-office of the council opened the spanish presidency by saying that he was aware of this weakness, that he wanted more, that he wanted to strengthen economic governance. and i ask you now, mr president of the european council, what was so gallant? what was so inventive as they brought? what's left of those purposes? in the matter of financial regulation, one bad news and two good news. the bad news is that the council has decided to delay the regulation of alternative investment funds - what was called casino capitalism - precisely at a time when these funds have been partly responsible for speculation against the greek economy. the two good news is that strategy 2020 talks about forcing financial institutions to make a buck to pay for some of the plates that break, or as obama would say, to prevent main street from paying for wall street's destruction, and the second is that the council for the first time singles out the systemic institutions that it wants to give special attention to. these two things are in the reports which parliament is now debating. they are not in the agreement reached by the council in december. i would like the european council to take up these two ideas, the strategy and the council, because then we will be much closer to dancing the tango. and believe me, mr president, i am very much looking forward to dancing it with the council you preside over.

mr president, i would like to congratulate mr van dalen and also my colleague mr fleckenstein on this brilliant initiative, which advances the european parliament's ambition in the field of the european union's maritime policy, and i would also like to thank them for their generosity in accepting a good part of my suggestions. the report thus completed includes such important issues as support for the adaptation of ports and vessels to the needs of people with reduced mobility, the requirement for ratification of the ilo maritime labour convention 2006 - and also calls for the industry to incorporate it into its practices - and the extension of vocational training proposals to all levels of the shipping industry to combat their undervaluation and exploitation. it also proposes leadership in the fight against pollution before the imo, both in the aspects of alternatives to bunker fuel and in the reduction of sulphur emissions, and suggests that this be done by using intelligent transport systems such as the galileo satellite system. the report also proposes to recognise the increase in the european fight against piracy and to support the increasing effectiveness of operation atalanta, as well as the requirement to improve the quality of the design of the vessels to adapt them to the highest requirements of accessibility and safety. finally, i am particularly pleased that the role of ports in the new transeuropean networks has been recognised, including their crucial connection with inland ports and logistics platforms.
