the next item is the debate on the oral question to the commission on specific measures for agricultural markets, by mr paolo de castro, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development (o-0036/2010 - b7-0208/2010). mr de castro is not present, so mr le foll has the floor.
member of the commission. - mr president, i think that the debate we have just had shows us how much we must learn from this milk crisis, and as mr le foll also said at the beginning of his speech, we should consider the establishment of market regulation mechanisms within the framework of the common agricultural policy after 2013. i sincerely believe that the common agricultural policy, while taking account of the diversity of european agriculture, must be able, in the context of the common objectives which we have at european level, to propose measures which will enable us to fulfil the role assigned to the cap in the framework of the lisbon treaty, namely to guarantee the stability of farmers' incomes and to ensure a good supply of markets. the future cap instruments must therefore be able to achieve these objectives, among others. of course, there are other goals, but these are the main ones we should consider. the measures to regulate markets, which will enable us to avoid or intervene in situations of price and market volatility, will be the subject of our concerns and the proposals that the commission will make in the context of the common agricultural policy after 2013. i can assure you we're working on it. i am firmly convinced and aware that, alongside the direct aids which we must maintain, while adapting the criteria for their distribution, market management mechanisms must be able to play a role. of course, the market must be able to function. we must let the market function when it can function, but i also agree with mr dantin when he says that the specific nature of the agricultural sector justifies public intervention. of course, it must be timely and aim at correcting the way the market works and making it work. it is in this spirit that we will make proposals for the common agricultural policy after 2013. i understand that other sectors are experiencing difficulties alongside the dairy sector. the fruit and vegetable sector is also often subject to strong fluctuations in the market: variations in prices and quantities marketed, quantities sold. this sector underwent a reform a few years ago. we will also learn from the implementation of this reform which gives producers more negotiating power within the producer organisation. i think that at this level too, it is possible to draw some lessons that we can apply in other sectors. i believe that in addition to public intervention, producers must also be given the opportunity to negotiate contracts better and thus to negotiate prices better, while ensuring a certain stability of the production placed on the market through private contracts. so beyond government intervention, i think we can find other ways that will allow the market to function properly, while giving the public authorities the power to intervene when the market cannot do its job, because agriculture must not only supply the market, but also continue to produce public goods. we're in agreement on that. so if agriculture is to be able to perform all its functions, it will need help. as regards food chain issues, in particular the negotiating powers for a better distribution of added value, work was carried out by the european parliament, the commission made a communication and there were discussions in the council. on the basis of all this, i think we will make proposals to find mechanisms which will enable producers to negotiate their margins better. i think i have covered pretty much all the speeches and all the issues that have been raised. i thank you again for the opportunity to speak. the debate is just beginning. i have launched a public debate before making proposals on the reform of the common agricultural policy after 2013. i think that as a result of this debate and the work that is going on in parliament, we will be able by the autumn, when i come back with a commission communication on the future of the cap, to make proposals that will give farmers more confidence in their work, in the farmers we need, not only in what they supply to the market, but also in what they achieve on their land.
the debate is closed. written declarations (article 149 of the regulation)

the rapporteur. - mr president, we are here today in the face of an important exercise for the liquidation of the 7th, 8th and 9th european development funds and the part corresponding to 2008 of the 10th european development fund, at a critical time, too, when important changes are taking place at institutional level and also when various global catastrophes have highlighted the growing importance of european aid and the need for it to be coordinated, effective and, above all, also transparent so that all citizens can continue to maintain their support and positive view of this aid. we are also at an institutional juncture where, with the implementation of the lisbon treaty and the creation of the post of high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy and the european external action service, a double opportunity is presented: on the one hand, the possibility of substantially improving the implementation and effectiveness of our external aid, but on the other hand, also some big questions, because we are concerned about the high risk that the increasing and difficult effectiveness we are achieving together with the court of auditors and the commission for european development aid could be undermined by a new reorganisation, the ambiguity of decision-making and the chain of responsibility and, above all, by fragmented management. we therefore need more assurance from the commission to avoid such lapses and therefore we need clarity and concrete action as soon as possible on what the new system will look like and how it will affect development aid. firstly, in connection with the current year, i would like to stress the need to incorporate fully - and this is the demand, i repeat once again - the european development fund in the budget in order to strengthen its coherence, transparency, effectiveness and control mechanism. we therefore 'stress' that the commission, together with parliament, should firmly maintain this demand for the next financial perspective. on the other hand, it is also important to strengthen joint programming to achieve greater concentration, coordination and vision in the work. and we therefore need to concentrate the 10th european development fund on a limited number of sectors. but, on the one hand, avoiding the harmful effects of proliferation - but, watch out, watch out, without undermining the capacity and effectiveness of the ngos on the ground, which are effective - is important, it is a complex exercise of squaring the circle, but we hope that, together with the commission, we can carry it forward. we are also pleased that the declaration of assurance has been positive, except for the corresponding commission's estimates of expenditure. there are no significant errors in the underlying operations, although we are still looking at and therefore needing to improve some important non-quantifiable error ratios, both in commitments relating to budget support and in payments. we are also very concerned that, once again, the court of auditors has not been able to access important documentation on payments representing 6.7% of the annual expenditure on cooperation with international organisations. we need a definitive method and an ad hoc timetable to ensure that the information and documentation of this joint funding is not undermined by this lack of transparency. we also consider that the financial implementation has been satisfactory, as the 7th european development fund has been closed and its balance transferred to the 9th; we also welcome the rapid implementation of the 10th european development fund as of 1 july 2008; and we hope that the commission's efforts will culminate in the settlement of the remaining old and outstanding payments. resources are another important point. we are also concerned, although there has been some discussion, that the resources of the 9th and 10th european development funds, which are managed by the eib, are not covered by the statement of assurance and should therefore be the subject of a regular report by the eib.

rilke was the favourite poet of our colleague dimitris tsatsos, who died a few days ago, and it was in this very house, a long time ago, on 19 november 1997, that dimitris tsatsos and i had the honour of presenting the report on the treaty of amsterdam to this parliament. and it was precisely in that report on the treaty of amsterdam that we proposed that any revision of the treaties should therefore be prepared in advance by a convention. we call this the community method, and it is this method of the convention that has been used to prepare the charter of fundamental rights and, above all, the constitutional treaty. i would like to recall dimitris tsatsos today when we are about to carry out the first reform of the treaty of lisbon, which, after all, mr president, is the constitutional treaty we have fought so hard to achieve. the first reform, which will affect the amendment of protocol no 36 to the treaty of lisbon, is motivated by an anomaly, because at the time of the elections to this parliament, in june last year, the treaty of lisbon had not yet entered into force, because of the visits that we all know. the last parliamentary elections were therefore held with the treaty of nice in force, and the treaty of nice provides for 736 members, compared with the 751 provided for in the treaty of lisbon. to complicate matters further, mr president, the 1976 act provides that members' terms of office are five years. this means that we cannot simply apply the provisions of the treaty of lisbon, the 751 because a given country loses, with lisbon, three elected members who cannot therefore leave parliament during this term. that is why, mr president, protocol no 36 must be amended to allow the lisbon agreements to enter into force and that during this parliamentary term, during the period 2009-2014, when the amendment to protocol no 36 enters into force, this house will have, exceptionally, 754 members. the european council has therefore written to you, mr president, asking you, in accordance with article 48 (2) of the treaty, to give parliament a ruling on two questions. firstly, is a convention necessary to prepare the amendment of protocol (no 36)? and the second question is: can the heads of government convene the intergovernmental conference to amend protocol (no 36)? the two issues are linked, although they are two separate reports. i shall begin by calling the intergovernmental conference. as i said before, this is the political result of the application of the treaty of lisbon, and it is a transitional and exceptional solution which will only take place during this parliamentary term. the intergovernmental conference will therefore stick to something that has already been agreed: how those 18 meps are distributed among the 12 countries. so there is no debate, mr president. i believe that the intergovernmental conference can be convened very quickly and resolved even in the course of a morning, since the political decision has already been taken. i shall therefore ask for the intergovernmental conference to be held and i shall say that i do not think it is necessary to have a convention on a subject which has already been settled. we are in favour of the opening of the intergovernmental conference; we are against the convening of a convention.
on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, i would like to begin by saying that this is not a minor decision we are taking on this occasion. we are, first of all, reforming the treaty. for the first time since it came into force, we are proposing a reform of the treaty, and this is no small thing. but secondly, what we are doing is to give back and confirm, to make possible the exercise of this right by 18 members who would have had the right to be members if the treaty had been adopted before the elections and by 12 countries which have the right to put their situation back together in this parliament, because they have agreed with the whole of the union to be more represented than they are. it is only that, but it is an important question. the council, with its good judgment, asks us: is it necessary to organize a convention in order to ratify an agreement by all the countries of the union? and what parliament is telling you is that it is not really necessary. this time it's not necessary. and it therefore mandates the council to convene an intergovernmental conference so that the treaty can be reformed, thereby opening the way for the 27 countries to ratify it, for the 18 members to come here and for the 12 countries to be fully represented. this is what we're trying to do, but there's been a problem. i would like to begin by acknowledging that we have had a difficulty in determining whether those who are to come must be directly elected for these elections or can be elected in another way. this problem which has arisen and which must be addressed and presented in its reality, i think has been solved in a satisfactory way. i would like to thank not only the rapporteur, mr méndez de vigo, but also mr duff, for the agreement we have reached between the three groups, which i think is very important. what we are saying is: yes, let the treaty be reformed, let it be done without a convention, so that the right to confirmation can be introduced. but at the same time parliament reminds the national parliaments that they must send directly elected members to the european parliament and that it is our vocation to carry out, within parliament itself, a review of the european electoral system in order to give the european electoral model a system of unity, of supranationality, in the way of electing members. these two considerations have brought about a balance which i am very pleased about and which allows us to restart this dossier.
acting president of the council. - madam president, i just wanted to add that i agree with those speakers who have expressed the importance of resolving this outstanding issue of the lisbon treaty, namely the 18 members who are not here because the last elections were held shortly before the treaty of lisbon came into force. the reform of protocol 36 is therefore worthwhile. i also agree with those who have expressed the view that this must be done as soon as possible, that the absence in this house of 18 members representing citizens from 12 countries of the union must be covered as soon as possible. that is why i am in the final analysis in agreement with mr méndez de vigo, who proposes that there should be no need for a convention, that the intergovernmental conference should be convened as soon as possible, that parliamentary ratification should be carried out as soon as possible in the 27 member states, and that we should therefore be able to see in this parliament as soon as possible the 18 members who should have been here since the beginning of this parliamentary term.

acting president of the council. - mr president, almost all the members who have spoken have expressed their support for the signing by the european union of the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. we're matching them. i would like to refer to the two speeches which i have heard which seem to me to show reluctance or opposition to that signature, on the understanding that it was either dangerous for the union's powers, as in the case of mr ziobro, or that it was unnecessary, as in the case of mrs morvai. i would like to refer to both of them and answer both of them specifically. as regards mr ziobro's argument, there is no problem with the strasbourg court being able to interfere with the union's powers. that's not his goal. this is also stated in the treaty of lisbon, protocol (no 8). it is clear that this does not change the powers and responsibilities of the union institutions. there's no problem with that. and, moreover, one of the issues being discussed in the working party on this subject is, alongside the question of the so-called co-defendant mechanism - that is, the union of the european union plus a member state - when there is an action before the strasbourg court against that state, the issue of the exhaustion of remedies, previously before the luxembourg court before going to the european court of human rights. that is one of the issues on which the working group is currently working at a technical level, precisely so that there can be no doubt that the european court of human rights does not fall within the competence of the union; it merely ascertains whether or not there has been a violation of the european convention for the protection of human rights. the second argument is that of mrs morvai, who says: 'i can go against a decision of an authority in my country and i can go to the european court of human rights; why do i need the european union to sign?' i think it is quite clear: the european union has powers which the member states do not have. the european union not only has powers, but has also increased them. the european union has become an institution which takes decisions through directives, regulations, decisions from a legal point of view, which may violate the european convention for the protection of human rights. and that is precisely why the european union's path towards an increasingly powerful institution makes it necessary - and why the treaty of lisbon states it this way - that just as the member states sign the european convention for the protection of human rights and submit to the jurisdiction of strasbourg, the european union must, in that logic, submit to the jurisdiction of strasbourg. on the other hand, the history of the european court of human rights and its case law has been highly positive for the rights of individuals in europe. the european convention for the protection of human rights, which is the text applied by the court, is quite old, dating from 1950, like the treaty of rome; this convention is also from rome. then it's been supplemented by some protocols. it is an old one, and yet there has been a very rich body of case law which has transformed the case law of the constitutional courts, of the supreme courts of the member states, and has constituted a kind of common doctrine which is what is essentially being established for the future in the interpretation of fundamental rights between the court of luxembourg and the court of strasbourg. we therefore believe that the european union has every reason to sign this convention. and we also believe that it will protect not only the citizens of the member states but also those citizens who come from outside the european union and have the status of foreigners, because the european convention for the protection of human rights protects anyone who is under the jurisdiction of a member state, if, in the future, under the jurisdiction of which any of the decisions taken by the european union are affected. therefore, not only nationals of member states but also non-nationals of member states will be protected by that convention if the union signs it. i am pleased to see that there is a consensus on the importance of moving forward with the mandate presented by the european commission; that there is going to be a session announced by mr jáuregui in the european parliament on this subject - and i take this opportunity to congratulate him and the other rapporteurs on this report, mrs gál and mr preda - and i would point out that the spanish presidency's intention is that this mandate, on the basis of the text sent by the commission - we understand that whoever negotiates this text with the european council - should be approved by the council of ministers, called the jha council, justice and home affairs, on 4 june next.

in this sense, as in so many other things, it is very important that the response to these challenges be given above all from a european perspective, with a european approach. within the industrial sector, we must place particular emphasis on the sectors with the greatest potential for growth and, without a doubt, one of these is the automobile sector, with its great capacity to transfer technology to other activities, its impact on employment, its export capacity, its growth potential. it is therefore important to focus on the automotive sector, which, according to the european commission's own figures, is a sector which directly or indirectly employs 12 million workers in europe and is the main private investor in r & d & i, with eur 20 000 million a year. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european car industry is not left behind. we are talking about the electric vehicle, which is one of the best examples of the innovative strategies to be considered in this sector. the spanish presidency has therefore placed the development of the electric vehicle at the top of its agenda as a preferred alternative means of transport to reduce dependence on fossil fuels derived from petroleum in the transport sector and thus move clearly and decisively to an energy-efficient and environmentally sustainable transport system. and for that we need a global strategy - that is what we think in the council - to develop technologies, including, in this case, electrical technology. the council is therefore promoting this debate on possible measures to be taken to boost the production of electric vehicles by european industry and that is why we are holding this debate at the informal council on competitiveness in san sebastian on 8 and 9 february. a really intense debate in which three main areas were identified for work: firstly, to promote a leading european market in the production of electric vehicles and their batteries; secondly, to support the adoption and acceptance of the electric vehicle as a means of transport similar to the conventional vehicle, to bring it up to that level or to try to have it at that level in the future, which it obviously does not have at the moment and will take some time to have; and thirdly, to create the conditions for a single market for electric vehicles to exist in this case too. it was therefore agreed to invite the european commission to draw up an action plan. in line with this invitation, the commission then will refer to it mr tajani has published its european strategy on clean and energy-efficient vehicles, a communication on 27 april, which discusses electrical technologies, other technological alternatives in this field and other issues. we would like to see conclusions drawn at the competitiveness council in may on the commission's communication of 27 april. that is our intention in that respect. in short, we believe that we must follow the objectives of this strategy and, within it, those of the 2010-2012 action plan, so that the broad lines of action are translated into 15 concrete actions, also proposed by the commission, to lay the foundations for the implementation of the electric vehicle.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, mr secretary of state, mr lópez garrido, as the spanish presidency mentioned in its speech, last week the commission, ladies and gentlemen, adopted a the commission's strategy to the house: the strategy includes over 40 concrete actions and i take this opportunity to outline the three that have been identified by stakeholders as the key priorities that the commission must address, namely standardisation, financial incentives and research. the standardisation of electric vehicles is of key importance in order to ensure that european citizens can charge their vehicles when crossing borders; the so-called interoperability is an essential requirement for consumers to accept new technology without reservations and thus to ensure the mass market deployment of electric vehicles. the commission therefore proposes that the commission work with the european standardisation bodies, following the established standardisation process, to adopt a single solution for interoperability, address safety risks and examine an intelligent charging system for the electric charger in vehicles. the standard must take account of existing technical solutions and, of course, guarantee consumers safety and affordability. i am convinced that we must take advantage of the momentum to opt for a genuine single european solution based on our internal market principles. if we miss this opportunity, we could find ourselves in a fragmented market for many years to come, which would not only be bad for european consumers and businesses, but also unwise in the face of the many competing international initiatives. as regards financial incentives, several member states have already introduced them. in some cases the incentives are explicitly for electric vehicles, while in other cases they are linked to low co2 emissions. the commission does not intend to oblige the member states to offer incentives, but it does want to coordinate the exchange of information and propose a series of guidelines in this area in order to avoid market fragmentation. the third element is research: the commission intends to work towards european research to achieve the goal of clean and energy-efficient transport by supporting research in all those technological areas, while streamlining and simplifying the procedures for obtaining european grants. i would like to conclude by stressing the impact that this strategy will have and that it goes far beyond the automotive industry. i share the spanish presidency's position: we are here to study a the dangers that this can entail for people. i think it's very important to consider his reflection. the technology used by the electric vehicle is also the most efficient and has the most environmental advantages. the efficiency level can reach 60% of the technology used for the electric vehicle, while traditional motors have an efficiency of 20%. on the other hand, in the field of energy, the electric vehicle objectively helps to achieve these objectives, which we were talking about this afternoon when we were talking about europe 2020 and the objective of combating climate change, the so-called 20/20/20 objective. the electric vehicle, which has storage capacity, has a technology that allows to soften one of the problems, the negative or weak points of renewable energies. the electric vehicle helps renewable energies, which have a weak point: they are irregular. the electric vehicle compensates for this irregularity by its special characteristics. and also, as far as energy security is concerned. many european countries do not have oil reserves, for example, and the electric vehicle could make up for that shortfall, helping to achieve what is also a strategic objective of the union: the fight for energy security, which we have seen that sometimes makes our societies deeply vulnerable. finally, i would say that, despite this, despite these advantages, we must admit that the electric vehicle will force us to change many of the manufacturing structures, including the technological ones i have mentioned above, the habits of citizens, the distribution networks of the source of energy for propulsion, and it will even make it necessary to go to a new communication strategy, as mr van nistelrooij said very rightly. it has many advantages, but it also has many obstacles, it also has many difficulties, and this clearly leads us to the need to give it a definite european perspective, to give it special attention by the european governments, the commission and this parliament, which will vote on a number of resolutions tomorrow. that is why it is so important that these three institutions of the union - the council, the commission and the european parliament - work together on the strategic line on the electric vehicle.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i believe that the spanish presidency has perfectly framed the electric car strategy in a wider, broader context, which is not just about the electric car but also about the development and defence of the automobile industry, in the context of european industrial policy, looking at what industry and industrial and employment development will be in the coming decades. this choice, which the commission shares, is therefore based on a twofold strategy, which certainly does not exclude serious work to reduce co2 emissions from conventional vehicles, on two pillars: the commission has already made a number of proposals to improve the safety of the car, the hot-air vehicle, which must be improved and so it is right to the next item is the debate on - the oral question to the commission on the protection of consumers' interests in the competition rules for the motor vehicle sector in the internal market, by malcolm harbour, andreas schwab, evelyne gebhardt, cristian silviu buşoi, adam bielan, heide rühle and kyriacos triantaphyllides, on behalf of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection (o-0044/201 b7-0209/2010) and - the oral question to the commission on the motor vehicle block exemption regulation, by sharon bowles, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs (o-0047/2010 b7-0210/2010).
vice-president of the commission. - mr president, first of all i would like to thank not only you for your excellent presidency of this sitting but also all the members who have spoken in this debate. i am very grateful to you, not only for your speeches today, but also for all your contributions, which have been extremely interesting and important for us throughout the process, which, as i said in my speech, has been a long process of consultation - if i may say so - in all directions; not only consultation with parliament, with the members of this parliament and with the committees of this parliament responsible for the problems of the car, of competition for dealers, of consumers, but also consultation with the member states, consultation with all the sectors involved and with all those who have wanted to express their views. the aim of any competition rules, any competition decisions, is to benefit the consumer. and that is the goal, the core of our concerns and the purpose of our regulation. consumers, as they approach the decision, important -- because, as some of you have said, it's a very important expense for every consumer and every family -- to go to a distributor, they want to know the price and the quality, compare, and that can be done, and probably can be done now better than at any time in the past. they want to be able to choose without the hindrances and obstacles of lack of competition. we believe that with the new regulation this choice will be extended, not reduced, but extended. and they can and should be able to choose - as many of you have said - after-sales services, the workshop where they can repair their vehicle, where they can check that the vehicle is working properly; they want those workshops, whether or not they belong to the manufacturer or are linked to the manufacturer of the vehicle, to have the appropriate technical information and to have the spare parts and the necessary specifications. all this is improved by the commission's present proposal. it all gets better. i would like to ask you to pay attention to the text you know, the draft, the draft and the guidelines, the accompanying guidelines. in all these respects, the future regulation will provide more advantages for consumers than the current one. small and medium-sized enterprises: what has happened? because we have to listen to opinions and we listen to them with a lot of attention and interest. everyone's opinions and, of course, those of your honourable members. but what has happened to the small distributors over the years? have they increased or decreased? have they been favoured with greater opportunities to enter the distribution circuit, the distribution market or have they been disadvantaged or encountered obstacles? more like the second. and that's the experience. it was not, of course, the will of those who drew up and decided the regulation in 2002, but it is what experience has taught us in recent years. and that's what we want to correct. what has been happening or is happening with certain workshops or with certain manufacturers of car spare parts? they have difficulties which will disappear with the new regulation and the new guidelines. we are therefore proposing a regulation and guidelines which will facilitate the possibilities and opportunities for small businesses along the whole chain, from the manufacture of parts to the repair of vehicles. the distributors, whom many of you have mentioned and whom i have also heard directly, not just through texts of written consultations or meetings in which i have not participated; i have been with them and have been talking to them, in an extraordinarily constructive meeting... not all distributors have the same interests. there are large distributors, with a strong market presence in some of the member states, but there are also many small distributors who are more happy with what we are proposing now than with what has been in force since 2002, because they have seen that certain aspects, not wanted by the legislator of 2002, have not benefited them, but have created difficulties for them to compete with the large distributors. and finally, the deadlines for withdrawal. we provide protection, we even provide exceptions for every time we consider that, with the current regulation, both the vehicle regulation and the general vertical agreements regulation, despite our will as legislators, competition suffers, and we can derogate from the application of the regulation if we see that it is not protecting competition. we can do this in the general regulation of vertical agreements and we can do it in the specific regulation of vehicles. so i share your concerns. the fact is that i think they are better dealt with in the proposal for a regulation than they have been so far, not because we are smarter now than we were eight years ago, but simply because we all learn from experience. you have to listen to opinions, but you also have to learn from experience.

member of the commission. − mr president, the commission very much welcomes your interest, support and valuable recommendations on mobilising ict to facilitate the transition to an energy-efficient, make sure that this potential is embraced and made a reality. the commission intends to make a priority of this issue under the european digital agenda which will be adopted soon by the european commission. as you mention in the report, ict can help to significantly improve energy efficiency in other areas, such as buildings and transport in particular. we also concur with you that smart grids and the roll-out of smart meters by member states are key to realising this potential. the roll-out needs to be driven forward within member states, so as to deliver more active consumers who can exploit renewable generation and energy-efficient technology. a common measurement framework for the ict industry’s own emissions is also essential. a rigorous measurement framework, widely agreed and adopted by the industry, is a must to quantify the real benefits of information and communication technologies. this must be taken into account in considering the beneficial impact of ict used. since the adoption of the recommendation on this topic in october 2009, the commission has undertaken a number of actions with stakeholders to drive the agenda forward. let me mention a few that address concerns raised in your report. in february 2010 the ict for energy efficiency forum was launched. the forum brings together leading eu, japanese and us high-tech industry associations. they will set targets on the basis of a common measurement framework for the ict sector’s own energy and carbon footprints, to be developed by the end of 2010. the forum is also looking at the contribution the ict sector can make to improve the efficiency of other sectors, such as building and transport. major european cities have signed up to the green digital charter. these cities commit to reducing their own ict carbon footprints by 30% by 2020, and to deploying five large-scale ict pilots per city by 2015. the total number of cities committed to the green digital charter has increased from 14 to 21. energy retail market issues are becoming increasingly important, as markets move closer to consumers, to the introduction of new technology and systems in the form of smart meters and smart grids. work with the commission’s smart grids task force is also advancing. the aim is to advise the commission on policy, a regulatory framework, as well as to coordinate the first steps towards the implementation of smart grids under the provisions of the third energy package. a set of recommendations is expected by the end of 2011. to conclude, let me emphasise that the commission is very committed to contributing to achieve the 20-20-20 targets by 2020 as set by the heads of state and government, and ict has an important role to play in this. we thank you for the valuable input provided by your report and look forward to cooperating with you to ensure that we adopt a good policy to achieve these targets.

president of the european investment bank. - mr president, i would like to thank all the speakers for their comments. of course, a number of issues raised would merit further discussion. i can only give a few answers here, distinguishing between questions which relate to our operational priorities and those which relate more to control and governance. as regards our operational priorities, one of them has caught the attention of many of you, and that is the support to be given to small and mediumsized enterprises. this was emphasized by mrs györi and mr schmidt among others. i think they are right to stress the importance of supporting smes. as you may know, we launched in 2008 a new product for bank loans to small and medium-sized businesses, which allows us to better track the use of the funds we lend. i can tell you that from the last quarter of 2008 to the end of 2009 we signed loans for 21 billion, of which 16 billion were actually disbursed and, at the end of last year, more than 90% of these funds had already been actually loaned to small and medium-sized enterprises. so i think that there is a significant support that can be provided through this channel, through the commercial banks, including, as mrs györi has stressed, not only the traditional commercial banks but also the regional banks and savings banks as intermediaries. we've diversified the range of our intermediaries. we are also trying to work closely with our subsidiary, the european investment fund, in combined operations, as this fund can provide guarantees to the sme loan portfolio. mrs auconie has given a very concrete example of this participation and i thank her for her words of support in this regard. the second operational priority that has caught your attention is of course convergence, and i can confirm that the european investment bank is working to increase its operations in the so-called convergence regions. so you will see that in 2009 our lending volume grew more in the new member states than in the old ones, with a determined will to try to help narrow the gap between member states, because that is the spirit of convergence. in this context, as mrs kadenbach and mr czarnecki have stressed, it is important to have good cooperation with the commission on the use of the structural funds, and i can tell you that this is the case. we have also developed with the commission several joint programmes: jaspers, to provide technical assistance for the preparation of projects eligible for the structural funds; jeremie, which is an original idea to transform the structural funds into financial instruments with a revolving character (the same amounts can be used several times); and finally, jessica, which is the same idea of using the structural funds for funds in the field of urban renewal. third operational priority: energy and the fight against climate change. we may have the opportunity to discuss this in more detail, but i can assure you that the idea is good, in line with the strategy agreed at european level, to put more emphasis on renewable energy and energy efficiency. mr lamberts cited figures for the period 2002-2008, but if you look at the most recent figures, particularly in 2009, you will see that the proportion is reversing, since in 2009 we financed renewable energy projects for more than four billion, which represents more than 70% of our financing for electricity generation. the intention is therefore to continue this reversal of the ratio by increasing funding for renewable energy and energy efficiency, and i thank the speaker, mr stavrakakis, for his reference to the elena programme, which is again a joint programme with the commission to provide technical assistance in the field of energy efficiency. i would also like to say to mrs benarab-attou that we respect the choice of each member state as regards the policy mix. if a state decides to use nuclear energy, the eib has no right to oppose it, but i can confirm that in the case of jordan we are only discussing financing for renewable energy. quickly now, a few questions relating to control and governance. as regards supervision, mr audy has returned to it, he knows our position, we are quite open, we are already largely controlled by an independent audit committee, by the court of auditors when we use the european budget, by olaf, by the european ombudsman. i think we're the most heavily regulated international financial institution. that said, i do recognise that having banking supervision could be useful, and so we are quite open to proposals that could be made in this area, particularly through the new european banking authority. as regards basel 3, i simply tell mr rübig that we are following the work closely. it is too early to say what the impact might be, since we are only at the consultation stage on basel 3 and the parameters are not yet settled. as regards offshore centres, i would say to mr geier that this is something that has attracted a great deal of our attention. if he wishes, we could explain our new policy in more detail, but really, the concern is to avoid tax evasion through the use of offshore centres. finally, a particular point raised by mr schmidt. he is right: we have progress to make on gender equality. the figure he quoted is for executives only. it is true that we have far too few women in the executive ranks of the eib. we have put in place an action plan and we hope to correct this situation in the coming years, but i want to assure you of our willingness in this respect to improve a situation which, as it stands today, is indeed unacceptable.

in writing. − my vote in favour of this important directive is due to the need to improve the energy efficiency of buildings, one of the areas with the greatest potential to contribute to the eu's overall objectives of increasing energy efficiency by 20% by 2020. the text, agreed by the european parliament and the council, states that by the end of 2020, all new buildings must be zero-energy buildings, producing as much energy as they consume. public buildings must set an example by complying with this regulation by 31 december 2013. the eu budget will finance part of the costs of the reforms. in addition, existing buildings will have to meet higher energy efficiency standards calculated by member states on the basis of a common framework established in the directive. the indicator for measuring the energy efficiency of buildings shall be included in advertisements for sale or rental in the media. another important innovation is the requirement to include smart meters and energy-saving control and management systems. the directive will be reviewed before 2017.
in writing. today's vote on eu rules for the energy performance of buildings is a major step forward in energy efficiency. however, we strongly regret that the legislation does not take into account the renovation requirements of existing buildings, which account for 40% of energy consumption and 36% of greenhouse gas emissions in europe. instead of implementing an ambitious energy efficiency policy by investing heavily in the renovation of buildings, the eu is focusing solely on new construction. it misses the opportunity to create millions of jobs, reduce our energy dependence on our neighbours and significantly fight climate change.

the rapporteur. - madam president, madam minister, commissioner, since dr christiaan barnard said that phrase 'jesus, dit kan werk' which in afrikaans means 'jesus, this is going to work' as he looked with disbelief at the beating of the heart he had just implanted, until today, 43 years have passed in which transplanting a useful organ from a human being who no longer needs it to another who needs it to live has become a daily practice. but it is no less true that this daily practice has not yet prevented the fact that there are now 56 000 europeans on the waiting list and that, of these, 12 may have died by the time this debate is over because they did not have the organ they need. and that is precisely the challenge for this parliament, which has to approve in this house both the directive, which dr mikolášik has explained so well, and the action plan. the aim is to provide broad, clear and effective channels for european solidarity so that no citizen of the union dies from lack of organs, and that this lack of organs is due to deficiencies in the transplant system. the increase in the life expectancy of europeans, the reduction in road accidents and the advances in science are certainly things to be celebrated, but they also make it necessary to make more organs available because there are more people who need them. the response of europeans when asked whether they would be willing to be a donor to save the life of a fellow citizen is highly positive. and if that willingness is not often directly reflected in the number of transplants that are carried out in each country, it is certainly because we need to improve our transplant system in essential aspects such as coordination, information, vocational training and citizen education in this area. examples of when coordination and training work optimally, the number of transplants per million increases, we have in some countries. and let me give you the example of spain, where a model of compulsory reference has been consolidated. the quality and safety guarantees in transplantation, together with the complementary, free and voluntary nature of in vivo transplants, which, as has been said, is established by the directive, are supplemented by the recommendations set out in the action plan on the need for continuing training of professionals, information and education of society in this field, without which it is difficult to work. all this forms the basis for optimising what we might call a european system of transplants, harmonized and shared by all the member states, as an instrument for achieving the objective we have set ourselves, which is at the moment to achieve the day when no european dies from lack of the organ he needs to live and that lack is due to systems which are not perfected. we cannot allow ourselves in the europe of the 21st century to have a situation where, because of a lack of coordination or of optimized systems, an organ is lost and another european human being cannot benefit from it. this is what is achieved by the adoption of this directive and this action plan, which is not a random effort. i would like to take this opportunity to highlight the good will and the good cooperation that has existed at all times both in the rapporteurs - in this case, mr mikolášik - and in the alternative rapporteurs, as well as the strong impetus that the spanish presidency - represented by the spanish minister for health and by dr matesanz, as director of the spanish national transplant organisation - has given to this directive and to the action plan, because we have been able to count on them at all times. i would like to thank the commissioner for his work and ask him to approve the report unanimously. i am grateful for the work as a member of parliament and i am grateful as a european for taking this step to save the lives of all the citizens of this union who may at any time need it.
madam president, commissioner, madam minister, i would first of all like to highlight the work of the rapporteurs, mr mikolášik and mr perelló, and all the efforts they have made to achieve the best possible compromise in favour of a transplant policy in the european union. i would also like to highlight the contribution of the spanish presidency and dr matesanz, director of the national transplant organisation of spain, because spain is currently the world leader in donations, with 34.4 donations per million inhabitants. this is entirely due to the continuous improvement of the organisation and the measures taken to raise public awareness of organ donation. the same thing must be achieved for the whole of the european union: increase the number of donations, ensure that all transplants are carried out within the same quality standards and, in addition, promote collaboration between all the member states of the union. we must also ensure that all donations are voluntary and unpaid, with the exceptions mentioned by commissioner dalli, in order to combat organ trafficking, which is entirely linked to organ shortages. the action plan can contribute to this by helping to address the shortage of organs and improving citizens' access to transplants. the solution reached for live donors is very important, since we cannot forget that live donations are complementary and have proved effective even when there is no genetic relationship between the donor and the recipient.
madam president, i want to congratulate you all on this initiative because it means improving the life expectancy of many people and making solidarity and fraternity more than just words. the basque country euskadi holds the world record for organ donation. in 2009, we had a rate of 38.5 percent donations per million people. thanks to this, we perform 60 kidney transplants and 30 liver transplants per million inhabitants annually. in the united states, the figures are 54.7% and 21.4%; in europe, 35.1% and 13.4%; and in spain, 48.8% and 24.6%. the success is due to the protocol applied in hospitals to attract donations and to a track record of organisation and awareness-raising - the two ideas to be pursued - as well as to the work begun as early as 1986 with the creation of the regional transplant coordination system: another example of how regions can make their contribution to europe.
madam president, madam minister, allow me to begin by saying that i come from cantabria, a small spanish region with a rate of 61 donations per million inhabitants, the highest in spain and europe. i would like to congratulate mr perelló and mr mikolášik on this report and for supporting this proposal for a directive which is designed to respond to the shortage of organs in the european union. the success of the spanish case is a model that can be useful for the rest of the european union with elements such as the competent national authorities, the traceability of organs or donations between living people. i would also like to congratulate the spanish presidency on its strong support for this issue as one of its priorities. ladies and gentlemen, you know that almost 56 000 patients are currently on waiting lists. donation rates and organ availability vary considerably across european countries. the lack of organs is a key factor affecting transplant programs. the good practices that can be achieved yield much greater benefits in some member states than in others. that is why - and i end by saying this - the adoption of this report is essential to improve the situation in all the member states.

member of the commission. − madam president, following the very good collaboration between the commission, parliament and council, i am convinced that we have now reached agreement on all the key issues. i would like to again congratulate and thank dr mikolášik and mr perello rodriguez for their contribution. i believe that by ensuring high quality and safety standards for human organs the proposed directive will be of great benefit to european patients. the directive will provide a comparable safety standard across the union and increased trust in transplantation systems. i am convinced that the proposed directive strikes the right balance between citizens’ data protection and organ traceability, and indirectly contributes to the fight against organ trafficking. this is not the solution to all the problems in the area of organ transplantation; this directive provides the framework, clarifies the boundaries of responsibilities and sets some standards. however, more needs to be done in the area of organising our hospitals, collecting and disseminating information, proper characterisation of organs and action against illegal trafficking. in the latter context, traceability will go some way to redress this, but this depends on the enforcement exercised in member states. member states are being given a great deal of flexibility, and we hope that all member states will give this issue the importance it deserves. the competent authorities that they need to set up should be adequately equipped and resourced to ensure proper data collection and control, traceability, supervised standards, characterisation of organs and in transplantation and conduct effective vigilance to report adverse events and reactions which will help all of us to minimise risk in the future. president, minister-in-office of the council, honourable members, from the contributions of the honourable members during this debate it is evident that the compromise text which is on the table today responds to everybody’s concerns. thank you for your input, your cooperation and your support. the rapporteur. - madam president, the fact that, at a time of difficulty and crisis such as those which europe and the world are going through, this parliament was able to adopt the first directive at first reading after the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon speaks volumes about the sensitivity of this parliament, reinforces confidence in democratic institutions and suggests that members of this house want to move forward and progress at the same pace as science and with the same degree of will and solidarity as european society. i do not know whether we have done everything too well or whether we could have done something else, but i do want to clear up any doubts that may have been raised. what i am quite sure of is that if we comply with everything we are going to pass in this house, we will be giving more life and we will be preventing the union from being able to commit any crime of organ trafficking, as it can be committed anywhere else on the planet, which is not the case at all in the european union. so if any of those doubts have been left in the mind of someone - and have been said by other colleagues - i want to clear them up. that was not our job. we have tried to respect the conscience of each individual, the ethical standards, the moral standards, without losing sight of the fundamental objective: that not a single european should be left without a transplant in order to live, because we can achieve more and therefore less organ trafficking. i therefore conclude that i do not know whether our work has saved all consciences, but i am fully convinced that we will save many lives. and that was our job and that's what we did.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i know that there are many important days in this house, but i sincerely believe that since the lisbon treaty was adopted on 1 december 2009, the mandate for the european union to join the convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms is one of the great news in the process of european integration and construction. i believe that we are therefore witnessing the culmination of an old aspiration which is part of the historical fabric of european construction, because human dignity, human rights, democracy, the rule of law are part of the dna of what has been, to a large extent, the historical fabric of european construction. this report, which we shall be adopting tomorrow, is the fulfilment of the mandate which the european union has had since the treaty of lisbon imposed this accession. and i would like to sum up the content of this report around three big ideas. on the one hand, i would like to remind you that it is not just the member states that protect human rights, but that it is now the european union - with its new legal personality under the treaty of lisbon - that it is community law and the development of the community state that can be achieved by the member states, that it is the principles of the european convention that are subject to a court outside the union and the member states that ensures, always and everywhere, that those principles are respected. secondly, the introduction of a new law and a new court for european citizenship, for european citizens: the right of citizens to have recourse to this new court to ensure that the rights established by the convention are respected in relation to the european union or to the member states when they develop community law. the activities of the european union's foreign policy, the police, security beyond our borders, international cooperation are also subject to the principles of the european convention on human rights. what's this all about? it is a great step forward, historically speaking, in the process of integration, in the construction of the most essential notion of the european idea, which, as we said before, meets the requirements of european citizenship and human dignity. it also means strengthening the european system for the protection of fundamental rights, because, together with the charter of rights and the treaty of lisbon, it establishes a universe, a framework of legal protection that is almost perfect and, of course, the most advanced in the world. it also strengthens the union's credibility vis-à-vis third countries, from which the european union has always demanded respect for human rights in its bilateral relations. this report deals with institutional and legal aspects which i shall not go into. what i want to stress is that a procedure is now being initiated here, because the commission - and i would like to thank mrs reding for the speed with which they approved the negotiating mandate, and the european council, which will do so shortly - has already, together with this report which has been prepared jointly by the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs and the committee on foreign affairs - and i would like to thank mrs gál and mr preda for their cooperation from these committees - an orientation, a negotiating framework, which will enable a negotiation to take place that will enable this parliament to return to approving that treaty and will enable the countries to ratify accession to the european convention. a great news, i think, ladies and gentlemen.

the rapporteur. - madam president, i would like to express my gratitude to all those who have spoken, because they have all, by a large majority, almost unanimously, expressed a very favourable position on the accession agreement which we are going to vote on tomorrow. i would like to thank mrs reding in particular for giving us the opportunity to continue working together because, indeed, a very complex negotiation is coming and i think that this parliament has to be very close to that negotiation. i would like to answer a few questions and make some clarifications very quickly. the accession is not a symbolic act, ladies and gentlemen, it has legal value. some wonder what it does, what it adds. i'll give you an example. let us say that a competition for european union officials discriminates against lawyers in hungary, let us say, for some technical reason or whatever. where do lawyers in hungary turn? the court of justice. what does membership add? the possibility for such lawyers to have recourse, if their right to equality has not been recognised by the court of justice, to the strasbourg court. it is a new court, it is a new opportunity to guarantee fundamental human rights, for example, that of equality. the contribution of this fact is therefore clear, not symbolically but legally. two points, your honour. the members of parliament have expressed the wish that the negotiation should not be limited to accession to the european convention on human rights, but should incorporate the protocols which the convention has been building up over the years, especially those relating to the rights recognised by the charter of fundamental rights, as this would effectively give an equivalence between the two documents. and finally, parliament is also called upon to join the bodies and bodies of the convention and the council of europe, because this will allow for recognition of the universal system of protection of human rights, including the european social charter of turin.

mr president, it was necessary to meet in the face of the abyss and the economic collapse so that the heads of state and government would understand that the way forward is not more nationalism but more europe. this is the direction in which some of the measures adopted are heading, such as the decline in the right of veto in the european council or the creation of a european public treasury. finally, though belatedly, we have learned that we are all sailing in the same boat and that it is useless to attend to individual situations and, moreover, to do so in an improvised way. but i wonder whether this attitude is a parenthesis or, on the contrary, the beginning of a real european economic government, because what is left, ladies and gentlemen, is governance, and what is missing is genuine government, if we are to be faithful to the will of the founding fathers. that is why we must, from this parliament, push forward all those reforms which are aimed at strengthening europe and making budgetary and fiscal discipline a reality, forgetting, by the way, nostalgic sovereignty. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval, and the council's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval.
mr president, the current parliamentary term began a year ago and there has not been a single sitting in which we have not discussed the crisis. and it is true that we have nothing more important to do than to talk about a crisis that has destroyed 20 million jobs in europe. but it's very important that we get the object right, because a wrongly stated equation is an equation of impossible resolution. the crisis is not the 'euro crisis in greece'. it is a crisis which has brought to light three intolerable asymmetries which must be addressed. the first is the asymmetry between the real and the financial economy. the second is the asymmetry in monetary union and the absence of a fiscal, budgetary and economic policy union that is commensurate with the requirements of monetary union. and thirdly, the virulence of the crisis and its challenges and, nevertheless, the exasperating slowness of the response and decision-making mechanisms that characterize the european union. that is why we are late in responding to all those millions of unemployed people who are watching us and we are raising difficulties that do not arise in other countries facing the crisis with greater decision-making capacity. we have seen extraordinary decisions at the same time: the commission communication, the extraordinary decisions of the council of ministers last weekend and, of course, strategy 2020. but these extraordinary measures are not free, they are accompanied by strong demands, restrictions and threats of sanctions against countries which are not able to restrict spending and therefore may also compromise growth. yesterday we were discussing here in the european parliament the european convention on human rights and the stockholm programme action plan. and we had the opportunity to recall that europe is not made only of the internal market or monetary union, it is not made mainly of that, but of citizenship, and so this is the moment to recall, once again, that these millions of european citizens are expressing their dissatisfaction with this europe that we are offering them, with this europe that expresses more threats and sanctions to countries that do not comply than incentives to a growth model that is able to bring them back to employment, to social cohesion and to the fight against poverty. without this europe of the people, this crisis will be an impossible crisis to resolve.
mr president, i believe that the worst crisis we can suffer is not only the one we are suffering today, but the one we will suffer if we are not able to draw the appropriate political lessons from what is happening to us. we have lived beyond our means, especially in some countries. we've moved away from the real economy and embraced the fictional economy, in our public accounts and, at the same time, in our family and private lives. we have not been able to understand that, as in any living organism, growing is not the same as getting fat. growth requires effort and proportion, whereas that process of getting fat is disproportionate and imbalanced to the effort we put forth and the well-being we enjoy. this crisis is dynamic. the picture of the crisis a few months ago was different, completely different, from today. and the one in a few months' time is going to be radically different from today. this crisis was economic and financial and will have an increasingly social dimension, of social conflict and, therefore, at this stage, before the conflict is social, we who are engaged in politics must know that our main crisis is a crisis of confidence. it's not just the euro crisis. let's analyze all the political and electoral processes in these months. there is a crisis of confidence and this means that what we have to ask ourselves is what we have to change, what is the change in attitude, what is the change in political, institutional, personal attitude, that we have to develop. and in that sense, this european parliament, instead of thinking of others, of other institutions, the question that has to be asked is what is its contribution to a change of institutional and political attitude in this house. and i dare say that today, having heard many reasons for the crisis -- bureaucracy, agencies, governments -- there are two issues where we need to change. firstly, europe demands a minimum of cohesion from this parliament: it cannot be allowed to bleed into such a profound debate on two conceptions of european society. and second, we have to dare to tell the truth about what's happening to us.

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, first of all i would like to thank the contributions of the alternative rapporteurs and their assistants, the secretariat of the committee on regional development, the secretariats of the political groups, as well as the cooperation of the dg regio and the employment dg of the european commission, the european economic and social committee, the committee of the regions, the trade unions and the associations and networks of european regions. in the course of preparing this report, i have held meetings with a number of regional and institutional associations, in particular the committee of the regions, the conference of peripheral maritime regions, the assembly of european regions, the network of regions for research and innovation, the european economic and social committee and the european commission, in their directorates-general for regional development and employment. i would like to thank all of them for their availability and their interesting contributions. following the change of title to include the reference to the europe 2020 strategy, the main objective of the report is to defend cohesion policy as a strong, well-funded policy that is present in all regions of the european union, and its key role in the europe 2020 strategy. the report was adopted almost unanimously in the committee on regional development: 40 votes in favour, 1 abstention and 1 vote against. the first part of the report briefly analyses the contribution of cohesion policy to the lisbon strategy and recalls the limits to the involvement of regional and local authorities, social and economic actors and civil society in the lisbon strategy, which made it difficult to take ownership, communicate and make it effective. the report also calls for evaluations not only of actual expenditure but also of its real impact. the second part is devoted to recommendations for the future europe 2020 strategy and highlights the importance of regions, multi-level governance and the partnership principle, basic pillars of cohesion policy which should be incorporated into the europe 2020 strategy as a necessary precondition for its successful implementation. it is also essential to strengthen the involvement of economic and social actors and civil society in general, in order to avoid the disconnection and discrediting of the strategy by its main actors. this part emphasises the key role of education, training, research and innovation, the importance of facilitating the implementation of the so-called knowledge triangle and the need to support small and medium-sized enterprises, which in many cases play a pioneering role in innovation. but at the same time, the specific needs of the regions and social groups with the greatest difficulties must not be forgotten, and a certain amount of flexibility must be allowed. to enhance the leverage effect of investment in r & d, education and training, we advocate the need for increased synergies between national strategic frameworks and national reform programmes, as well as greater coordination and coherence between the various european, national and regional policies related to the objectives of the strategy. the european investment bank plays and should continue to play an important role through financial engineering and cooperation instruments and support for regions and small and mediumsized enterprises, but in order to facilitate its task and that of all beneficiaries, further progress towards simplification is necessary. in conclusion, the report advocates a strong cohesion policy for the future, well funded and present in all regions of the european union with a key role in the europe 2020 strategy.
mr president, i have to spend ten seconds telling my opponent to go to greece and ask there who is responsible for the problems the workers are suffering at the moment. they're not waiting for the e.p.d. no, not sir. they expect real policy change, such as strategy 2020 can bring about. if we do the analysis wrong, we'll have the wrong solutions. and the analysis we have to make is that europe is suffering enormously from greed, from lack of regulation, from lack of economic governance, from not having a sufficiently prepared, cohesive population, from not having social justice, from having low economic growth, from having low employment growth and from still having huge layers of the population outside the labour market and low skilled. the effort of the next ten years, mr president, must be to increase the number of people in work and to have people with much more education to win the battle of productivity. we will not gain competitiveness in europe without winning the battle of productivity. we will not win our place in the world by lowering wages, breaking social standards, but by raising the level of knowledge, raising the level of solidarity in our society, our social cohesion - these are our strengths - making europe a truly united continent, with a clear project, clear objectives, with an economic governance that not only allows us to respond to the urgencies of today, but also to the challenges of tomorrow. that is our hope, and it is the hope that a large majority of members in the committee on employment and social affairs have forged, leaving aside the siren song of those who want to go back and 'save your own life' and breaking solidarity between all. and that, mr president, is what we hope: that strategy 2020 will connect with the european citizens, who are asking us for more jobs, more quality jobs, economic governance, fiscal consolidation - yes, but also social consolidation and economic consolidation, because otherwise we will achieve nothing.
mr president, in the year 2000 we adopted the lisbon agenda with very ambitious objectives. some have come true, but many, many have not. regional funds certainly contributed to the lisbon strategy. ten years later we have been shaken by the worst economic crisis in our memory, and i believe that this has served to enable us to establish, in this new europe 2020 strategy, where we went wrong and thus improve in order to achieve better results. firstly, we have learned that coordination between all levels of governance is essential, as mr cortés' report very well said. we have also learned that the contribution of the regional funds is essential if we are to achieve the objectives we have set ourselves. we believe that the combination of concrete actions at all levels - european union, state and regional and local authorities - is absolutely necessary. if we work together, we'll be much stronger. it will also be important for the europe 2020 strategy to include a policy of economic, social and territorial cohesion. i would like to make a point here in connection with the subject of cohesion policy: the procedures must be much more flexible and much more efficient. and in the disability sector too, that difference will have to be covered in some way. finally, i would like to stress the important role that europe's regions and cities have to play and, in particular, the need to pay more attention to areas with special needs such as mountain areas, coastal areas or islands. in short, if we are to succeed, we must rely on europe's regions, cities and towns, and on a reformed cohesion policy adapted to the new situation.
mr president, commissioner, the future 2020 strategy must enable the union to correct the shortcomings identified in the lisbon strategy if we are to achieve a truly competitive economic area with economic, social and territorial cohesion. although the principles of the old lisbon strategy are still valid, i would like to stress that one of the reasons why it lost its strength was its highly complex structure and, in particular, the lack of clarity in the definition of responsibilities and tasks between the union and the other levels of government, especially regional and local. regions and local authorities must be involved in policy design and implementation if the future strategy 2020 is to bear fruit in the medium term. our regions and cities are the key actors in the development and implementation of a large part of the union's public investment in growth and jobs. the allocation of regional policy resources becomes a priority agent for achieving the european objectives we are defining. i would remind you that the resources invested between 2000 and 2006 through the european regional development fund have enabled the creation of 1 400 000 jobs in the union or the construction of more than 2 000 km of motorways. i would like to conclude by once again stressing the value of european regional policy in support of the strategic objectives of growth and employment. economic, social and territorial cohesion is a fundamental objective guaranteed by the treaties.
the rapporteur. - madam president, i would like to thank all the members for their contributions and for the constructive atmosphere we have maintained in this important debate. this report on the contribution of cohesion policy to the lisbon objectives and the europe 2020 strategy is one of parliament's essential contributions to the definition of the future europe 2020 strategy for growth and jobs, one of the priorities of the spanish presidency. the report emphasises job creation, the promotion of a sustainable economy, education and training to promote development, employment and competitiveness, and the key role of investment in research and development, taking into account the need to provide specific measures for regions with natural difficulties. but europe 2020 cannot be successfully implemented without the participation and full endorsement of regional and local authorities and civil society. the regions not only contribute to the co-financing of projects, but are able to take a much closer pulse to the needs of citizens and small and medium-sized enterprises, and to establish a direct link with universities and innovation centres, fostering the knowledge triangle. in this context, cohesion policy is not only a source of stable financial allocations, but is a powerful instrument for the economic development of all european regions. its objectives 'to eliminate existing disparities between regions and to bring about effective economic, social and territorial cohesion in europe' and its core principles 'an integrated approach, multi-level governance and genuine collaboration' are essential and complementary elements for the success of the europe 2020 strategy.
